title: IMB missionaries share vision for Seoul during Serve Tour
summary: Ask most people what comes to mind when they think of South Korea, and they’ll likely mention K-pop, skincare, cutting-edge technology, or bustling city streets filled with young professionals. Hun and Eunjoo Sol see those things too. But after more than a decade serving as International Mission Board missionaries in Seoul, they also see something many visitors never notice. “Many people think that Korea is exciting and successful,” Hun said. “They think about the K-pop, the K-culture, K-technol
content: Ask most people what comes to mind when they think of South Korea, and they’ll likely mention K-pop, skincare, cutting-edge technology, or bustling city streets filled with young professionals. Hun and Eunjoo Sol see those things too. But after more than a decade serving as International Mission Board missionaries in Seoul, they also see something many visitors never notice. “Many people think that Korea is exciting and successful,” Hun said. “They think about the K-pop, the K-culture, K-technology, K-cosmetics. Yes, good things… But many Korean people are struggling right now.” The Sols, who were featured in the 2025 Week of Prayer for International Missions , continue to rely on the prayers of faithful Southern Baptists. Prayers sustain them and help to push back the darkness they confront in their home culture. Hun often describes that hidden struggle with a Korean word: han. There is no simple English translation. It speaks to a deep sorrow shaped by generations of war, division, loss, and the quiet resolve to endure. Hun sees it in the young adults he meets every week—people navigating loneliness and relentless expectations, quietly asking what their lives are for beneath a veneer of success. Han is heavy. For many young adults, that weight can feel unbearable. Suicide is one of the leading causes of death among teenagers and young adults in South Korean. Hun and Eunjoo see the effects of that reality every day, and it’s one reason they believe they have no time to waste. That understanding shaped the week of Serve Tour Seoul this summer. There were no construction sites, no paintbrushes, no tools or work gloves. Instead, the team stepped into ministries local churches had been faithfully building long before the volunteers arrived. In May, 27 volunteers from seven churches across the United States came alongside local churches already serving their communities in Seoul, Paju, and Gwangju. They taught English classes, ran children’s camps, walked neighborhoods in prayer, distributed food, and sat down with college students, one conversation at a time. For Nick Holst of Sandals Church in Riverside, California, the goal was simple enough to say in a sentence: “We came to meet people,” Holst said. “We want to hear their stories, and that leads to some very meaningful connections as you get past the surface into something deeper.” That’s where the week actually lived: past the surface and past the small talk, where the quiet weight of han is often carried without words. On college campuses, volunteers played games, asked questions and mostly just listened. Some conversations lasted a few minutes and ended there. Others kept going long past the point where either person expected them to. One morning, after asking his church back home to pray, Holst sat down with a university student named Intec. They talked about culture first, the way strangers do, and then the conversation turned somewhere neither of them planned. “I got to ask him, ‘What do Koreans believe?’” Holst recalled. Intec said he didn’t believe in God. Then he recited John 3:16 from memory, word for word, a verse he’d heard somewhere along the way and never forgotten. Before they parted, Holst asked if he could pray that God would keep drawing Intec toward Himself. “He said yes.” In a city where many conversations never move beyond the surface, the exchange was a reminder of why the team had come. Not to win an argument, but to listen, to ask questions, and to trust God with what happens next. The same pattern unfolded elsewhere, beginning in classrooms and ending on city streets. Jeremy Doyle, missions pastor at Valley Baptist Church in Bakersfield, California, watched an English conversation club grow from two students on its first night to eight by the second. Nobody advertised it as anything more than a place to practice English, but the room kept filling, and so did the conversations. The team’s work with students didn’t stop there. title: Arrested at the hospital where he worked, he turned the prison into a pulpit
summary: 🇪🇷Eritrea· 2010s
content: Dr Berhane was a new believer in Jesus, working in a hospital in Eritrea, when the secret police came for him. His crime was his faith. They put him in prison for eleven months, in one of the harshest systems on earth, a place designed to make Christians disappear and go quiet. He did the opposite. "Every day I was clapping my hands," he said, "and prisoners would come forward and I shared the gospel." A man who had only recently met Jesus decided his cell was simply the next place to introduce Him. Three Bibles and a valley of death The authorities took his Bible. He smuggled another in. They took that one too, and he smuggled a third. He leaned hard on the Psalms, and when fellow prisoners were taken out and executed, the old line about walking through the valley of the shadow of death stopped being poetry and became the thing that held him upright. Eleven months of that did not break him. It made him a preacher. The guards meant to silence a new Christian and instead handed him a congregation with nowhere to go. Wherever they put you, Jesus goes with you, and He is not intimidated by the walls. Dr Berhane found that out in an Eritrean prison. You can trust it wherever you are.

title: A construction engineer in Madagascar became convinced the Bible was true
summary: 🇲🇬Madagascar· 2013
content: Melias was building things for a living in Madagascar, a construction engineer with a steady trade and, by his own account, no particular expectation that God would interrupt him. In 2013, at twenty-one, God did. It was not dramatic thunder. It was quieter and harder to argue with. "The Holy Spirit convinced my heart that the Bible is true," Melias said. "I found new joy and excitement learning about Jesus through the Scriptures." The book he might have dismissed became the most alive thing in his life. From building houses to building the church He could have kept his new faith as a private comfort and gone on with engineering. Instead he gave it everything. In 2015 he trained for six months as a missionary, and since then he has planted churches and discipled new believers among the Tanala people in Ikongo and the Sakalava in Nosy Be, some of the least reached corners of the island. Now he is training three more Malagasy missionaries to do the same. Madagascar is not a footnote in what God is doing. He is raising up local people like Melias, engineers and tradesmen and ordinary workers, and sending them to their own unreached neighbours. When the Holy Spirit convinces your heart that this is all true, it does not stay a hobby. It becomes the thing you build your life around. He is ready to convince yours.

title: A New Testament sat in his welding workshop until a teenager finally read it
summary: 🇳🇪Agadez· 2000s
content: Someone left a New Testament in Pierre's welding workshop in Niger, and for a while it just sat there. He was a teenager, and eventually he picked it up. What he read did not match what he had been told about Christians. It was full of tenderness, of nearness to the poorest, exactly the kind of world his young heart had been quietly hoping was real. Years later he moved to Agadez, out toward the desert, and there he found the thing the book had described. A church family drawn from Benin, Togo, Burkina Faso, France, and Niger, living out what he had only read about. No regret, not for a single day Pierre became a lay missionary, and he does not hedge when he talks about it. "I have never regretted converting to the Christian faith," he says, "not even for a single day." That is a bold thing to say in Niger, where jihadist groups make following Jesus dangerous and his own children have stayed Muslim, something he carries with love and without pressure. Still, no regret. Not one day. He read about a God who is tender toward the poor, and he found that God to be exactly as advertised. Whatever you have heard about Jesus secondhand, He holds up when you finally meet Him yourself. Pierre would tell you to open the book and see.

title: He was taught Christians do not pray. Then he watched his uncle pray before a meal
content: Charles Yabaga Diarra grew up in a strict Muslim family in Lere, Mali, where Christians were mocked and misunderstood. His father, a headmaster and politician, ran the house like a school. As a boy, Charles fled about a hundred and fifty miles to stay with an uncle, and there he ran straight into something he had been told did not exist. His uncle, a Christian pastor, bowed his head and prayed before the meal. Charles was stunned. "Because we are Christians, we pray before meals," the uncle explained. Charles had been taught that Christians do not pray at all. That simple prayer, in his own language, lodged in him and would not leave. Just show me the way His father pulled him back and forced him into Quranic school, but the seed was planted. Years later, back with his uncle, tired and searching, Charles finally prayed his own prayer. "Lord, I'm really tired of seeking the truth. Just show me the way." A verse he had heard at a Vacation Bible School came back to him, and in November 1981 he gave his life to Jesus. The cost has been real. Charles is a preacher now, displaced by Mali's conflict and facing daily pressure. But he did not go alone. Of his fourteen siblings, most now follow Jesus, and around a hundred Christians gather at his extended family events. One uncle praying over dinner turned a whole family toward Jesus. Your quiet, ordinary faithfulness may be planting more than you know.

title: A widow heard the good news from a travelling salesman and could not unhear it
summary: Laos· 2022
content: Pei was a fifty-two-year-old widow in Laos, raised the way her whole village was raised, worshipping ancestors and local spirits in a place where the government pushes atheism and neighbours warn that following the God of foreigners will offend the gods of home. Then a salesman came through and, somewhere between selling his goods, told her about Jesus. Salvation as a gift, not a payment. Pei believed it. She let go of the ancestor worship she had carried her whole life and quietly followed Jesus instead. The cost at her own front door She was discipled in secret for four months, growing strong enough to speak. The first people she told were her daughter and her son-in-law, who happens to be a policeman. They did not celebrate. He threatened her, saying that if she did not stop believing in Jesus, they would report her, jail her, or throw her out. In June they made good on it, tossing her clothes into the yard and telling her to go live with the people who gave her this Jesus. She went. She did not go back. A widow with nothing chose Jesus over a roof, because she had found something no one could evict from her heart. Following Jesus is not always safe, but it is always worth it. What Pei found is worth more than what it cost her, and it is offered to you too.

title: After his daughter was killed, he prayed for a Bible no one could take from him
summary: Uzbekistan and Tajikistan· 2020s
content: Rashid Kadirov was a Muslim in Central Asia when the worst thing happened. His six-year-old daughter Azizza was killed by a drunk neighbour driving a tractor. In his grief he went looking for something the ache could rest on, and he went to the Koran. There he read a line, in Surah 5:70, that pointed back to the Gospels as holy scripture. So he prayed a strange, specific prayer. He asked God for an Injil, a New Testament. His friends brought him one. It was a stolen Gideon Bible, taken from a vandalised car. It did not last. When the friends took it back, Rashid prayed again, this time for a Bible no one could take away from him. The book that stayed Then a couple arrived from Tajikistan, sent by a former classmate of his who had himself come to Christ. They carried a Bible and a copy of the JESUS Film. Rashid and his wife Aleka watched it, and as the good news was explained, each of them, without telling the other, quietly prayed to receive Jesus. Aleka barely understood it all. "She had very little understanding of the Gospel," she said later, "and yet peace flooded her heart." They were baptised in Tajikistan, and Rashid started telling others what he had found. A grieving father asked for a book, and God gave him a Person. The peace Rashid could not manufacture arrived the moment Jesus did. He is close to the brokenhearted, and He is near to you.

title: 35 priests could not help her. In a church she saw Jesus crush what was choking her
summary: 🇱🇰North Central Province· 2021
content: Chandra lived in a rural village in Sri Lanka's North Central Province, and she was slowly falling apart. Pain, weakness, a heart that raced for no reason doctors could name. She and her family were Hindu, so they did what they knew to do. They went to priest after priest. Thirty-five of them. Nothing changed. In July 2021 they walked into a church instead. As people prayed for her, Chandra saw something. Demons were trying to strangle her, and then Jesus Christ stepped in and stamped on them. She felt the pain and the sickness drain out of her body as they were defeated. In the vision Jesus spoke Scripture over her, from Psalm 34. "They looked to Him and were radiant," He said, and told her she would be radiant too if she trusted Him. The prayer a father prayed Her husband Dinesh, a day labourer, watched his wife come back to life and made God a promise. "God, if you will heal my wife, I will dedicate my daughter for your service." The whole family, who had barely heard the name of Jesus, gave their lives to Him. Their daughter Tenusha told her class what had happened, that her mother was free and that Jesus forgives sinners and makes them new. They did not keep it to themselves. A house church started in their home with four people. By now it is forty-six. Jesus is still stronger than whatever is choking the life out of you. He steps in, He stamps it down, and He calls you radiant.

title: He prayed for his mother's infected leg. Then his Muslim neighbours started coming
summary: 🇸🇩El Hasahisa· 2022
content: Pastor Abdalla Haron Sulieman gathered his small church in El Hasahisa, Sudan, to pray for his mother. Aisha Adam was sixty, and a leg infection had worn her down. They prayed, and she recovered. What looked like a private family mercy did not stay private for long. Word of the healing moved through the town, which is mostly Muslim. And people started showing up at the church. Not to argue. To ask if the God who healed Aisha might heal them too. When a healing becomes a door That is exactly the kind of thing that makes some people afraid. Local extremists pressed the police to arrest Sulieman, and they did, charging him under an old law with claiming to be a witch doctor, as if the love of Jesus were a kind of sorcery. Believers across Sudan shared his name and called for his release. "This is a serious violation against Christians in Sudan," said one, an evangelist named Francis Ismail. But notice what the fear could not undo. A mother was well. A Muslim town had seen the name of Jesus do something real, and neighbours who had never entered a church walked in looking for Him. God still heals, and He still uses one ordinary answered prayer to open a door no one can shut. He can open one where you are too.

title: Karma said he had to earn heaven. At 17 he heard he could be forgiven
summary: Rakiraki· 1990s
content: Simon Gounder was born into a strict Hindu family in Fiji. His great-grandfather had been shipped from India as a contract labourer after the British took the islands in 1874, and the family settled in a small village in the north of Viti Levu. Simon grew up inside a system with clear rules. "As a Hindu, we believed in karma," he said. "If you do good karma, you get to heaven. If you do bad karma, you will be punished." It was a ledger he could never quite balance. He knew his own wrongs too well. The night the ledger closed At seventeen, a friend invited him to a Christian youth meeting in another town. There he heard something that did not fit anything he had been taught. That Jesus Christ could simply forgive sins. Not offset them, not average them out over lifetimes. Forgive them. Simon felt the weight of his own failures and, for the first time, an offer to be free of them. "I gave my life to Jesus that night," he said. He hid it from his parents at first. When they found out, they were not happy. But the son who came home changed did not stop there. In time he led his whole family to Christ, and he went on to plant a ministry that carries the same forgiveness to others. Karma keeps a running tab you can never clear. Jesus tears the tab up. Whatever you are carrying tonight, He is still in the business of forgiving it all at once.

title: A soldier who should have died in battle walked into a demon's shrine
summary: 🇲🇲Myanmar· 2010s
content: Pastor Dano was a soldier before he was a pastor. He came out of the battlefield alive when he had no reason to, and he never shook the sense of why. "I believe God preserved my life from death on the battlefield for a purpose," he said. The purpose showed up in a Buddhist village that wanted nothing to do with him. The vice chief's son was tormented, demon-possessed, and no one could help. Dano fasted and prayed for three days. Then, near midnight, he went to the shrine where the boy was and did the only thing he knew to do. "I called upon the name of the Lord," he said, "and the demon left the young man." The night the shrines fell silent Villagers said every evil spirit left the village at once. Dano went from shrine to shrine, praying against the darkness that had ruled the place for generations. The vice chief's family, who had braced for his anger, found grace instead. They gave their lives to Jesus, and four more families followed. The people who once opposed him now follow his lead. There is a church in that village today where there used to be shrines. The name of Jesus is still stronger than every dark thing that has ever frightened you. One believer, praying at midnight, was enough to set a whole village free.

title: They locked the pastor in a psychiatric ward. He led a hundred men to Jesus
content: Pastor Bakhytzhan Kashkumbaev was an elderly man when Kazakhstan arrested him in May 2013. The charges were strange, that he had harmed a church member's health and stirred up religious hatred. They sentenced him toward ten years and put him in a psychiatric ward, where inmates were routinely drugged. On the way in, he thought it might be the end of his mind. "This is probably the last time I will talk to you in my right mind," he said. Then a question reached him, the kind God uses. "Where is your faith?" Under the cover of the risen Lord Something lifted. "I felt like I was under the cover of the risen Lord," he said. The old man who expected to lose himself instead found Jesus nearer than the walls. He started talking to the men around him. To a prisoner wrecked by drug addiction he said simply, "Only Jesus can help you." Over nine months inside, nearly one hundred inmates gave their lives to Christ. "In prison," he said, "the Holy Spirit opened one dimension of prayer to me." The place meant to break him became the most fruitful pulpit of his life. They released him in early 2014. He walked out having planted the good news in the last place anyone would look for it. God is not locked out by any door that locks you in. He was already inside, waiting.

title: Her church offering came to the exact amount of her power bill, to the penny
summary: 🇺🇸United States· 2020s
content: Lina Johnson did not have enough to cover her power bill. She had told no one the amount. Not a friend, not her church, no one. It was her private worry, the kind you carry quietly and hope somehow resolves. That same week an offering came around at church for a family in need, and Lina gave what she could. Twenty-six cents. It was almost nothing, and she gave it anyway. Down to the penny The next day a friend told her the rest of the story. The offering the church had taken was for her. And when they counted it, it came to the exact amount of her power bill. To the penny. "The offering they took in church yesterday was for me," Lina said, "and it was the exact amount as my power bill. It was to the penny and I never told anyone how much my bill was." Here is the detail that undoes you. Had she given more than her twenty-six cents, the total would have overshot the bill, and the provision would have lost its edge. Even her small gift was part of God's arithmetic. God is not rounding up or guessing. He knew the number she never spoke aloud, and He met it precisely, through people who had no idea. The Father who counts the hairs on your head knows your bill too, down to the last penny.

title: He carried a bomb into a church. The sermon was about loving your enemies
summary: 🇮🇩Jakarta· 2000s
content: Ahmad Quraisy was a commanding officer in a militant Islamist group in Indonesia. The economic collapse of the late 1990s had radicalised him, and he blamed Christians for what had gone wrong. So he built a plan. He carried a time bomb into a Protestant church in Jakarta, intending to kill everyone inside. Then he heard the pastor preach. The man was telling his congregation to love their enemies and to pray for the people who persecuted them. Quraisy froze. "I never saw that Christian love before in my life," he said. He could not do it. He carried the bomb back out. His own leaders locked him up for a month for failing. The love he could not detonate That was only the beginning. In the year that followed, Quraisy began having visions he was sure came from Jesus. He was healed of typhus. His wife, unknown to him, had been quietly praying. By 2001 he gave his life to Christ. The man who wanted to blow up a church now builds them. Quraisy leads an underground network of around seven thousand former Muslims meeting in house churches across Indonesia, most of them still keeping a low profile to stay safe. The love that stopped his hand in that church is the same love reaching for you. It is stronger than the worst thing you ever planned to do.

title: He survived the killing fields. Then he baptised the man who ran a death camp
summary: 🇰🇭Cambodia· 1980s-1990s
content: Christopher LaPel grew up near the royal palace in Cambodia and wore a small ivory cross as a boy, though his father disapproved. Then the Khmer Rouge came. In 1975 he was driven into the labour camps, working sixteen-hour days in the fields. He lost both parents, a brother, and a sister to execution and starvation. He nearly died himself. When he was too sick to work for three days, soldiers came to execute him, and one of them looked at him and said he really looks sick, and walked away. He survived into a refugee camp in Thailand, empty and grieving. There a missionary told him that Jesus Christ had died on the cross for his sins. "This is the answer I've been waiting for," LaPel said, and he gave Jesus his life. The general who said, my sin is so deep LaPel became a pastor and went back to teach his own people. In 1995 a quiet man calling himself Hang Pin came to one of his leadership trainings. He gave his life to Christ, was baptised the next day, and began leading a house church. Only later did the world learn who he really was. Kang Kek Iew, known as Comrade Duch, had run S-21, the prison where around twelve thousand people were tortured and killed. He came to LaPel and said, "My sin is so deep." Duch surrendered to the authorities and was sentenced to life in prison, where he wore out the Bibles LaPel kept sending him. The man who survived the killing fields carried the grace of Jesus back to one of the men who built them. No sin is too deep for the blood of Jesus. Not the worst thing done to you. Not the worst thing you have done.

title: A witch doctor got a solar radio. It was tuned to the truth
summary: 🇨🇬Democratic Republic of Congo· 2010s
content: Mbutu was a witch doctor in a remote village in the Democratic Republic of Congo. For years he cast spells, claimed power over the natural world, and sold cures to sick villagers who had nowhere else to turn. People feared him. He made his living off that fear. Then he was given a small solar-powered radio. It was fixed to one station, a local Christian broadcast, and handed out to villagers who had no other way to hear anything. Tuned to the truth So Mbutu listened. Day after day the good news came through that little speaker. He learned of the One who really controls the universe, and more than that, he learned about the love of Jesus and His offer of forgiveness. The man who had traded in fear laid his witchcraft down and gave his life to Christ. He did not keep it to himself. Mbutu now walks from village to village, finding other witch doctors and telling them what he found. Some of them have become believers. Some have become pastors, planting churches where there were none. A cheap radio and the name of Jesus were enough to turn the most feared man in the village into its brightest light. No one is beyond the reach of that name. Not the person others are afraid of. Not you.

title: No Condemnation
summary: Featuring thousands of study notes drawn from the bestselling NIV Application Commentary series, the NIV Application Bible helps you understand Scripture and connect it to your world in a whole new way. It guides you in discovering how the ancient truths found in Scripture relate to your experiences today using insight from trusted evangelical scholars, paired with timely biblical application principles. Read an excerpt on the blog. See Also Free Stuff Fridays (HarperCollins) Using the NIV Zonde
content: This week, the blog is sponsored by Zondervan and this article is adapted from the NIV Application Bible . Text in bold is taken from the application notes on Romans 8:1 in the NIV Application Bible. Beneath the outer veneer of our lives, many of us live with a layer of guilt and shame. We feel like we’re not good enough. We want to be good Christians, but we just don’t feel like we are. Perhaps we sit in church surrounded by people who seem to have their lives more together than ours and who seem to lead better Christian lives than we do. This feeling leaves us anxious and ashamed, unsure of where we really stand before God. Let Romans 8:1 fill you with hope: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus”! Because we are justified by faith in Christ, we escape the sentence of spiritual death that our sins have earned. We have been transferred into the new realm of life. Because we have believed in Jesus’ finished work for us on the cross, we no longer have to fear that our sins will ever condemn us. Once we are walking with Jesus, we walk by faith and depend on grace rather than our own works. Our hope is not in what we have done or in what we can do, but in what God has done in Christ Jesus through his death and resurrection. If we are in Christ, there is no condemnation. If God does not condemn us, we must not go on condemning ourselves. Instead, we walk in the freedom and joy of God’s grace, led by God’s Holy Spirit. title: Who or What? A Continuum for Using AI Wisely
summary: From AI as god to AI as assistant. Here is a continuum of nine roles that can help Christians tell legitimate uses of AI from illegitimate ones, and wise from unwise. See Also A Christian’s Guide to AI Technology is Fast, Sanctification Is Slow, and Claude Can’t Do It For You Living as Christians in the Age of AI
content: It is sometimes hard to believe that it has been only four years since AI became widely available. Few technologies have made so massive and rapid a leap into our daily lives, to the extent that AI now exists in the background of all of our lives and, for many of us, in the foreground as well. Few technologies have evolved as quickly, so that the latest ChatGPT model bears about as much resemblance to its debut as the latest MacBook does to a Commodore 64. If all this has happened in just four years, imagine what the next four—or the next fourteen—might hold. As AI’s capabilities have increased, so too have the ways we can use it in our homes, churches, and workplaces. It seems like every month or two we read of a feature that can make a difference to our lives by adding a new ability or taking on work that used to be done by a person. The latest trend is the rise of agents—AI tools like Meta’s Muse or xAI’s Grok Bot that can carry out tasks, routines, and duties on an ongoing basis. With all of the tools available to us and all of their capabilities, it can be difficult to know which uses are legitimate and which are not. We all know that just because AI can do a task doesn’t mean that it should . So how can we determine the legitimate roles AI can play in our lives? I think sketching out a continuum of some of AI’s potential roles can help us. At the beginning are roles that most of us would agree are illegitimate, and at the end roles that most of us would agree are legitimate. Between them are roles that may be illegitimate in some cases and perfectly fine in others. These demand that we approach them thoughtfully to determine whether integrating them into our lives would be an act of wisdom or folly. As you will see, illegitimate roles tend to be those that require a who whereas legitimate roles tend to be those that require a mere what . The Continuum AI as God . There are some people, most of them deeply engaged in the tech industry, who ascribe to AI god-like qualities and who relate to it accordingly. They may believe it is an evil god that is likely to destroy humanity or a benevolent god that is likely to redeem humanity, but in either case, they treat AI as something far more than software. These people go too far and commit idolatry as they attribute to tech what rightly belongs to God. AI as Friend . There are some people who relate to AI as a friend, and even a few troubled people who relate to it as a lover. While AI is capable of mimicking the kind of relationship one might enjoy with a fellow human being, it can only ever mimic it. To relate to AI as a friend is to anthropomorphize a mere technology and worse, to deprive oneself of actual friendship. Though AI can imitate friendship, it cannot be a friend in any legitimate sense of the word, for friendship depends upon personhood. Not only that, but friendship depends upon mutuality and both the blessings and risks that come with relationship. You cannot be friends with AI any more than you can be friends with a tree, a PlayStation, or any other non-being. AI as Counselor . Many people today relate to AI as a counselor—a confidant who will listen patiently and counsel them with a trusted voice. Yet because AI is a what , not a who , it cannot offer answers based on a true understanding of their circumstances, true wisdom that comes from learning and experience, or true compassion that comes from sharing their humanity. It cannot empathize with them, pray for them, or plead with the Holy Spirit for wisdom in helping them. AI is capable of advising in many ways, but not of counseling, for counseling is inherently personal. AI as Pastor . Increasingly, people bring to AI the matters of spiritual health, growth, and well-being that in the past would have been addressed to a pastor. Every Christian needs to be under the loving oversight of a pastor who will care for their soul, and such crucial matters must be entrusted not to AI, but to a pastor who is called and

title: A La Carte (November 16)
summary: Can you keep falling into the same sin and still be a Christian? / Seven thoughts on how we change / To the man seconds away from watching porn / Does the Incarnation authorize images of Christ? / What is supernatural is not necessarily mystical / The heritage trees of the church / Kindle deals and more See Also A La Carte (December 23) A La Carte (November 13) A La Carte (October 24)
content: Good morning. Grace and peace to you. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include some seasonally appropriate choices from Crossway, like Come, Let Us Adore Him: A Daily Advent Devotional , Good News of Great Joy: 25 Devotional Readings for Advent , and Everyday Gospel Christmas Devotional . Remember that there’s a substantial November Kindle sale going on as well. If you prefer print books, then be sure to look at the Pre-Black Friday sale on a wide variety of books, many of them from Zondervan and Zondervan Academic. Recommended Reading Can You Keep Falling into the Same Sin and Still Be a Christian? This is a very good question and one all Christians need to ask when we assess our lives. “You’ve done it again. The very sin you promised yourself you wouldn’t commit. Perhaps it was an angry outburst. Another dishonest conversation. Another evening viewing pornography. Another moment of bitterness, gossip or pride. You knew it was wrong. You’d prayed about it. Perhaps you’d even confessed it to another Christian. Yet here you are again. And now a troubling question begins to form. ‘Can I really be a Christian if I keep falling into the same sin?'” Seven Thoughts on How We Change. This article by Jason Hsieh nicely complements the previous one. “Have you ever felt stuck on how to make progress with a particular struggle? Trying to change, repent, or grow in Christ can be a long, arduous road met with frustration, doubt, and discouragement. This post highlights seven factors that help us change. While it’s not exhaustive, it may give you and those whom you walk alongside ideas about what could be missing in your efforts.” To The Man Seconds Away From Watching Porn. And here’s one more piece on sin, though this one covers a specific form of sin. “The first germ of temptation drifted down long ago. Gradually, like snow gathering on a tree branch, the weight has quietly grown heavy, so very heavy; you feel you cannot hold it back any longer. So, here you are: browsing the Internet, hoping to ‘stumble’ upon something, anything, that will give you a justifiable excuse for succumbing. The dark monster of Lust is looking for an opportunity to swing you, branch to branch, from your typical Internet content to something more sinister, more secretive, more sensual.” Does the Incarnation Authorize Images of Christ? The issue of whether or not Christians should create images of Christ comes up often. Anthony Faggiano offers a very typically Reformed/Presbyterian response. “A recent discussion on X about a theological book cover raised a question that seems to come around every Holiday season. Reformed Christians objected to its picture of Christ. Roman Catholic participants raised an objection worth considering: because God became man, depicting Christ does not violate the Second Commandment. If God made himself visible at the Incarnation, why should Christians refuse to portray him? That honest question deserves a careful answer. Jesus truly became one of us. Yet I believe that his becoming visible didn’t give us permission to make pictures of him.” What is Supernatural is Not Necessarily Mystical. Michael Kelley distinguishes between the supernatural and the mystical. “Just because something is supernatural doesn’t necessarily mean it’s mystical. When we think of something being mystical, it’s a bit more hazy than something being supernatural. When we say something is mystical, we mean it’s obscure. It’s mysterious. And while the two words might share some characteristics, I’m thinking more and more that it’s important for us to recognize the difference because doing so impacts the way we live out our faith.” The Heritage Trees of the Church. title: Works & Wonders (November 15)
summary: This week’s Works & Wonders: a devotional on God’s sovereignty, Voyager’s light-day, Indelible Grace’s Draw Near, the Pano Awards, Codex, and octopus escapes. See Also Works & Wonders (Oct 11) Works & Wonders (September 27) Works & Wonders (April 19)
content: In my weekly Works & Wonders column, I combine a brief devotional with other interesting and uplifting bits and pieces I gleaned throughout the week. I hope you enjoy this week’s collection! It includes: All Will Bow: A Devotional Voyager’s Light Day Draw Near Pano Awards Codex How Octopuses Squeeze Through Heal and Make Whole 1. All Will Bow God is often described as sovereign. “Sovereign” is a word of royalty or kingship that describes one who has supreme power and authority within his rightful jurisdiction—both the right and the ability to act in the ways he sees fit. A king has the right to act only within his own kingdom, yet because God created the world and owns it and fills it, his dominion extends through all time and all space—through all that is and all that will be. It extends even to each human being, for all have been created by God and all, therefore, owe allegiance to him. As sovereign, God has purposed to have all bow the knee to him, their rightful ruler. And through his power all will, though in different ways. Some will see his word and his works, respond to his mercy, and bow in worship. Some will see his word and works, harden their hearts, and be forced to bow before him in judgment. But either way, all will bow before him. 2. Voyager’s Light Day NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft is about to mark its first “ light day ” as it reaches one light-day from earth—much farther than any human-made object has ever traveled. It will be 16 billion miles from Earth, having been launched in 1977. NASA has an invitation for you: after sunset on Tuesday, November 17, step outside and flash V-G-R in Morse code at the sky with a flashlight or phone, since VGR was Voyager’s call sign. While one light-day is a notable accomplishment, it may be worth pointing out that the edge of the observable universe is something like 47 billion light-years away, so we haven’t exactly caught up to the Lord. 3. Draw Near I didn’t see this one coming: the second Indelible Grace album of 2026. Yet here we have it: Draw Near . Like its predecessors, it is composed largely of retuned hymns from the past, though I believe there are some originals as well. (2026’s other album was Rove No More , in case you’d like to give it a listen as well.) 4. Pano Awards The photography competition of the week is the Pano Awards , which honors the best examples of panoramic photography. Panoramas will nearly always be landscapes, which is my favorite kind of photography. Not surprisingly, the results are stunning. 5. Codex Codex is a neat new initiative from the missions organization Missionary. I’ll allow the people who made it to explain it: “Codex is an index of unreached language groups (ULGs), people united by language yet strangers to Christ and His Church. By detailing who the unreached are, where they live, what they believe, and what stands between them and salvation, Codex fuels informed prayer for those who have not heard.” 6. How Octopuses Squeeze Through You’ve probably seen videos of octopuses squeezing through holes that seem far too small and, in fact, may be even narrower than the most rigid part of their body. Scientists recently put the effort into figuring out how they do it, and the answer is pretty interesting. Helpfully, they captured it all on video so you can see it for yourself. You’ll need to read Science News’s How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step to learn how they do it. 7. Heal and Make Whole I enjoyed this new live recording from of “ Heal and Make Whole ” from The Soil and Seed Project. It’s a whimsical telling of the life of Christ through trees. I guess you’ll need to give it a listen to figure out what that means. You can find the lyrics here if you scroll down. summary: Teach your children to hate you / AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework / Mobs and friends: encouraging a culture of reading in our churches / A Christmas care package for a Canadian WWII soldier was left behind / Christians shouldn’t invoke “the Longhouse” / 7 Ways to be a friend according to the Bible / Reader recommendations See Also Weekend A La Carte (August 22) A La Carte (August 14) Weekend A La Carte (March 29)
content: Good morning and welcome to Weekend A La Carte. Be sure to scroll down to read this week’s Reader Recommendations. I think you’ll find some good ones there! And check in again tomorrow for Works & Wonders. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include a wide selection of books. There’s more of the best of Crossway there, along with a large selection of C.S. Lewis, some classics, and more. Recommended Reading Kyle Borg writes about Luke 14:26 and the need to raise children who love the Lord even more than they love their parents. The Bible clearly teaches that the discipleship of children belongs primarily to mom and dad. That’s the ultimate priority of any Christian household. Everything parents can and should provide for their children is subordinate to discipling them to be followers of Jesus. That’s a significant responsibility. There are many things we can delegate to others: childcare, a measure of schooling according to conscience, and opportunities for others to speak words of guidance and counsel into our children’s lives. What we cannot delegate is the discipleship of our children. That remains the primary responsibility of every Christian parent. Read: Teach Your Children to Hate You. I suppose it comes as no great surprise to read that AI has made it almost impossible for universities to assess and evaluate coursework. It seems that every learning institution will need to adapt to the existence of AI by changing the way it tests and evaluates its students. Universities should go back to traditional exams and in-person presentations to grade students after lecturers complained that AI has made it “close to impossible” to assess coursework, according to an investigation by England’s higher education regulator. The Office for Students (OfS) said the credibility of degrees from England’s universities was under threat from the prolific use of AI in essays, dissertations and “open book” exams, with students reporting that their peers boasted of using AI undetected by staff. The regulator warned universities and other higher education institutions that failing to design “valid and reliable measures of students’ knowledge and skills” to combat AI could breach their conditions of registration and lead to sanctions being imposed. Read: AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework, regulator says. Jake Meador says, rightly, that “The easiest group for most of us to belong to is a mob.” That’s because “mobs do not require one to think. They do not require sacrifice. They do not require vulnerability. They do not require patiently tolerating another person, or seeking to understand the person. They simply require one to act—and to act in the same way that everyone else is acting.” Obviously mobs should be of concern to Christians. So what’s a superior alternative? Friendship as a form of community is almost entirely opposite to the mob. Mobs do not think or understand; they simply act. But in friendship we learn, through patient observation and conversation, to recognize another person, to understand them, even in some sense to think their thoughts after them. We learn to enjoy shared goods together, and to see the things that delight us in new ways precisely because our friend has taught us how. We sometimes say, “Oh, I wish so-and-so were here to see this,” precisely because we know they would love whatever it is we’re seeing. In friendship, we learn what it means to be human in a deeper way, what it means to share our life and our mind with another. Read: Mobs and Friends: Encouraging a Culture of Reading in Our Churches. What started out as an attic renovation of an English mansion has led to a revelation for the family of a Canadian soldier in the Second World War. title: Good News for Midlife
summary: A review of Jared Wilson’s Good News for Midlife, a candid, gospel-centered guide for men in middle age. See Also A La Carte (May 2) A La Carte (March 28) Weekend A La Carte (June 12)
content: I will be turning 50 in a few weeks’ time, and whatever else that may mean, it definitely means that I am now well into middle age. Now that I’m here, I feel like there were many resources to guide me when I was a young man, and there will be many to guide me as I become an old man , but not nearly so much that pertain to these middle years. Jared Wilson seems to have noticed this as well, and he did something about it by writing Good News for Midlife: Navigating Middle Age with Guts and Grace . Good News for Midlife Jared Wilson Buy from Amazon (Affiliate links) Midlife is a strange season in that we are neither young nor old. We are no longer just starting out, but we are also not yet near the end. While our work is well underway, we have not yet brought it to completion, and though we may see the end on the distant horizon, we are still in the game and still have a lot to offer. In its own way, it is a time that can be embraced or resented, that can be full of victories or full of failures. For some men, these will be the best of years, and for some they will be the worst. Wilson describes the season this way in his introduction: As men reach middle age, we face unique challenges related to physical and spiritual health, reckoning with our past, and preparing for retirement or the future in general. But while this season of life poses unique challenges in marriage, family, and health—not to mention in our thoughts about legacy, heritage, and “what it’s all about”—midlife also presents exciting opportunities to trust Jesus for personal, marital, and spiritual flourishing. Wilson has written this book for men who understand there will be new challenges and new blessings in these years and who wish to remain faithful throughout them. It is for men who want guidance as they approach these years and enter them, lest they fail to make them all they could be. To that end, he divides his book into two broad sections. In the first, he explains how to flourish now. He writes about the necessity of keeping the local church central to a man’s life since “real men are churchmen.” Men need to embrace their position in the life of the church and maintain a full commitment to it. He writes about marriage in the middle years as children gain their independence and the house grows empty. “The midlife marriage season—whether you’ve got older kids at home or you’re living together in that empty nest—is one that has proven challenging for countless couples. Many husbands and wives spend twenty years or more gradually relating to each other only as dad and mom, and when they’re suddenly given more time together, they don’t have any idea what to do with it. They look at each other and think, Who are you?” In this way, marriage becomes different from what it was, and wise men will learn to adapt to these changes. Parenting changes too as children no longer need their fathers to function in the ways they did in the little years. “When your children become adults and leave the nest, your role may change even further. You’ve gone from quarterback to coach and now to booster. Boosters wield some influence on the team, but it’s more in the way of support from the background. As many dads of adult children will tell you, they especially feel like an athletic booster in the area of ongoing financial support!” After covering parenting, Wilson covers work, friendship, and health, all areas that may be different in midlife than in other stages, but each of which is important to a man who is eager to embrace this middle stage of life. The book’s second part is a trio of chapters that look to the future and to finishing well. Here Wilson discusses legacy, lament, and endurance. Legacy considers the heritage a man wishes to bequeath to his descendants, lament honestly assesses and repents of failures, and endurance is finishing well, even if that involves finishing physically weak. He wraps it up with a series of very practical ways that men can honor the Lord

summary: Churches shouldn’t just ban Hillsong, Bethel, and Elevation / The new benefit of clergy / Everything sad coming untrue / What do we do with New Testament books not written by apostles? / The million dollar gene editing question / Scrolling the soul shallow / Kindle deals / The funnies See Also Weekend A La Carte (December 27) A La Carte (October 2) A La Carte (November 25)
content: Good morning from San Diego, where I’m speaking at a men’s retreat this weekend. This is my final event for the year, so I guess I’ll soon be settled in at home for the rest of the winter. Sales & Deals Yesterday saw the launch of a huge sale on Kindle books, most of which are published by Crossway. You can find that complete list on my November Kindle Sale page. Many of these books are cheaper now than I’ve ever seen them. Of course, there are some other Kindle deals as well which you can find in the usual place. Westminster Books has a great deal this week on R.C. Sproul’s commentary series . I have often found them useful. Recommended Reading Churches Shouldn’t Just Ban Hillsong, Bethel, and Elevation. Though I’m sticking with my perspective on the matter, I appreciate Kenny Klinglesmith’s alternative take on singing Hillsong, Bethel, and Elevation. “I’ve been leading worship for 15 years. For the past 10, I’ve served as a contract leader for multiple congregations throughout Texas. And increasingly, I’ve encountered churches all across denominational lines taking a strong position: They won’t sing songs written by the worship behemoths Hillsong, Bethel, or Elevation.” The New Benefit of Clergy. Writing especially of Russell Brand and David Walliams, Carl Trueman compares modern celebrity scandals to older clergy scandals. “Reviewing the autobiography of Salvador Dalí, George Orwell asked why moral monsters like the Spanish surrealist were granted immunity from accepted moral standards. His answer was that artists enjoy ‘benefit of clergy’—the medieval practice of granting clergymen accused of crimes the right to be tried in church courts, where penalties were considerably lighter than those faced by ordinary villains. The same holds true today. We grant our modern holy men, the artists and entertainers, a similar privilege…” (You’ll need one of your per-browser monthly allotment of free articles to read it.) Everything Sad Coming Untrue. “Gandalf! I thought you were dead! But then I thought I was dead myself. Is everything sad going to come untrue? What’s happened to the world?” Jacob Crouch explains why this little scene from The Lord of the Rings chokes him up. What Do We Do With New Testament Books Not Written by Apostles? Not all of the New Testament books were written by apostles, of course. Some people suggest this presents a problem when it comes to their authority or place in the canon. Michael Kruger disagrees. “In the end, it is fair to say that the entire 27-book corpus of the New Testament is apostolic . In some fashion, they all bear official apostolic testimony about Jesus and his message. Thus, they all bear the very authority of Jesus himself.” The Million Dollar Gene Editing Question. Emma Waters outlines two different forms of gene editing and explains why she regards them very differently. “In many of our conversations about technology, the question is rarely whether to ban a tool outright. The goal is to figure out how to use it for health, healing, and human flourishing, while banning or limiting the ways it can be misused.” This, she says, is the case with gene editing. Scrolling the Soul Shallow. John Piper does a good job of explaining what it means to have a shallow soul. “I have said many times that the worst problem with television (or now let’s just say Instagram or any online media in general) is probably not the pervasive sexualization of all of life — that’s big enough — but rather the pervasive trivialization of all of life. You can scarcely watch TV ads or be online for more than ten seconds without being dump-trucked with banality and silliness. Grown men and women, even famous grown men and women, act like eleven-year-olds whose high point at summer camp was to bob for apples in a toilet filled with Mello Yello — the apex of satisfaction. That’s the quality that we’re being dumped on every day.” The Funnies My friend Chris Martin maintains a Substack called The Funnies , and every Saturda

title: Spoiled for Choice: Two New Graphic Novels of Pilgrim’s Progress
summary: Two new graphic novel adaptations of Pilgrim’s Progress have arrived within weeks of each other. Here's how they are similar and different, and my recommendation of which one to buy. See Also A La Carte (July 27) The Puritans: John Bunyan A La Carte (6/3)
content: I have often expressed how spoiled Christian readers are today. As if we needed more proof of this, how about the fact that in a single month, publishers released not one but two major graphic novel adaptations of Pilgrim’s Progress ? Both are well-written, beautifully illustrated, and faithful to Bunyan’s story. Let me help you understand their similarities and differences and tell you which one might be best to add to your library. Christian’s Quest is written by Tyler Van Halteren and illustrated by Manuel Zepic. It is published by Lithos Kids, which has already released the three-part Little Pilgrim’s Big Journey , an illustrated adaptation of Pilgrim’s Progress for young readers, and The Mansoul Chronicles , which is based on Bunyan’s Holy War . It is a 220-page 7×10.63 inch hardcover that targets children aged 8+, though it is meant to be enjoyed by teens and adults as well. Its illustrations are what I might describe as a clean, polished YA style. The lines are thin and tidy and much of the form comes from shading. The colors tend to maintain a soft, muted, painted look. It lightly updates some antiquated language so that Bunyan’s Slough of Despond becomes the Bog of Despond. Christian is youthful and fresh-faced, and his burden is a bulging pack on a frame. It includes some bonus material: a behind-the-scenes look at how a graphic novel is made, and a study guide that explains and applies each of the stages of Christian’s quest. It also indicates that a sequel, Christiana’s Crown , will be released in 2028. Pilgrim’s Progress: The Graphic Novel is written by Jeremy Patenaude, illustrated by Brent McKee, colored by Matt Wilson, and lettered by Taylor Esposito. It is published by Crossway as what I believe is the company’s first graphic novel, though it has a long history of publishing books for young readers. It is a 256-page 7×10.25 inch paperback that targets readers aged 14+. Its illustrations are what I might describe as gritty and stylized and perhaps a bit more indie than mainstream. It uses heavy brush ink, dark shadows, and vivid colors. It does not update Bunyan’s antiquated language. Christian is a gaunt, tormented, weathered adult whose burden is a huge stone roped to his back. Its bonus material includes a lexicon of the key characters and locations and reflections on each of the chapters. There is no indication of a sequel that will cover Christiana’s quest. While these two graphic novels tell the same story and tell it faithfully using dialogue and illustration rather than narration, they tell it using different visual language largely because Christian’s Quest is meant to be accessible to a younger demographic. You might say that Christian’s Quest is a bit more kid-friendly and Pilgrim’s Progress is a bit more adult-friendly, though both could easily be enjoyed by kids and adults alike. After all, who doesn’t enjoy reading the occasional graphic novel? Another key difference is that Pilgrim’s Progress is a paperback where Christian’s Quest is being sold as more of an heirloom object that features cloth binding, gold foil, and a ribbon marker. Let me show you a few examples of the art from each book. Christian’s Quest These are drawn from the publisher’s preview images. Pilgrim’s Progress These are drawn from the sample chapter on Crossway’s site. My Recommendation Which do I recommend? Either! Both! If your readers are younger, Christian’s Quest is the more obvious choice, and if they are older—teenagers and up—they may prefer Pilgrim’s Progress . But you couldn’t go wrong with either, and you couldn’t go wrong with picking up both. Where to Buy Christian’s Quest Lithos Kids · clothbound hardcover · ages 8+ Buy at Amazon Westminster Books Pilgrim’s Progress: The Graphic Novel Crossway · paperback · ages 14+ Buy at Amazon Westminster Books See Also A La Carte (July 27) The Puritans: John Bunyan A La Carte (6/3)

title: A La Carte (November 12)
summary: On spouses sitting together in church / Can’t you just be like me? / Husbands, pray for your wives / Six comforts for pastors / The most fun I ever had / Will we really be perfect in heaven? / The most offensive doctrine / Kindle deals and more See Also A La Carte (August 1) A La Carte (July 4) A La Carte (February 12)
content: I hope you don’t mind that this is a bit of a book-heavy week, but I’ve had a lot of book content I have wanted to share. Hence, we’ve had This Week in Christian Books , The First 100 Books for the Children’s Section of Your Church Library , and Spoiled for Choice: Two New Graphic Novels of Pilgrim’s Progress . A book review will follow tomorrow, then we’ll be mostly caught up for now. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include P rioritizing the Church in Missions , Growing Up , and several good books for children. Recommended Reading On Spouses Sitting Together in Church. I happened to spot some of the kerfuffle that erupted after TGC Australia shared an article about why spouses should consider not sitting together in church. As happens on social media, the response seemed far out of proportion to the article. I found Murray Campbell’s response a good and reasonable one, even if I intend to keep sitting with Aileen most Sundays. Can’t You Just Be Like Me? I suppose in some ways, Bobby Scott’s piece on tribalism and disunity could nicely follow the previous article. “Tribalistic churches and Christians demand conformity to their broad range of preferences, believing they are inviolable God-ordained principles. So they strive to silence or coerce other Christians to assimilate, or they quietly despise these brothers and sisters. This inevitably leads to dark consequences. Instead of loving other Christians who have the same primary biblical convictions but differ over tertiary issues, tribalistic Christians feel justified in waging war against them.” Nelson’s Complete Book of Bible Maps and Charts is out in a fourth edition, updated with new high-resolution photography to go with its full-color maps, timelines, and charts for every book of the Bible. (Sponsored) Husbands, Pray for Your Wives. Costi Hinn: “I’ll never forget the first time I sat in a men’s Bible study on a Saturday morning listening to a man unpack the importance of praying for your wife. I was honestly blown away by the simplicity of it all and how I had never thought to pray for her — and I mean, like really pray for her.” He outlines eight ways men can do so. Six Comforts for Pastors. This article from Darryl Dash delivers what it promises. “If we base our identity on how well our ministries are going from an earthly perspective, we will be in trouble. Every pastor’s ministry will have good times and bad times. Basing our identity on how well things seem to be going is like putting our hope in a volatile stock. We will end up elated some of the time and despondent the rest. As pastors, we need to put our confidence in something more secure than how well things seem to be going. Here are six comforts for pastors that will last and sustain us, no matter how well or poorly our ministry seems to be going.” The Most Fun I Ever Had. Concerned about all those who are disparaging motherhood today, Brittany Allen chooses to celebrate it. “I still find it hard to write articles about the joys of motherhood because I never want to isolate sisters who are longing for a family. Yet, at the same time, I want to talk back to our culture that treats motherhood as a curse rather than a gift.” Will We Really Be Perfect in Heaven? Randy Alcorn: “Someone e-mailed me this question: ‘In Heaven, will some people still be annoying? After all, eternity’s a long time!’ Annoyance is sometimes caused by others’ sin, our own, or both. Since sin will be eliminated, so will annoyance. That doesn’t mean people won’t have idiosyncrasies, only that they won’t be rooted in sin, and none of us will degrade or dismiss others.” He explains what it means that we will be perfect in heaven. The Most Offensive Doctrine Every now and again, I like to share a quote that I have encountered through my reading. This is drawn from J.C. Ryle’s Expository Thoughts on Luke , which I’m enjoying a lot. Of all the doctrines of the Bible, none is so offensive to human nature as the doctrine of God’s sovereignty.
author: Tim Challies

title: Kehilangan yang Membawa Berkah
title_zh: 带来祝福的失去
content: Oleh: Gevonny Dinda Shalom! Perkenalkan nama saya Gevonny Dinda, biasa dipanggil Dinda. Sebagai orang Kristen, saya merasa bersyukur dilahirkan di dunia ini dan berkesempatan untuk mengenal Tuhan Yesus. Saya sungguh bahagia dapat merasakan berkat-Nya setiap hari dan sangat bersyukur akan apa yang Tuhan Yesus berikan kepada saya selama ini. Kabar baik, kabar buruk, cobaan, dan berkat, saya terima dengan penuh rasa ucapan syukur. Di sini, saya akan menceritakan salah satu berkat Tuhan dalam kehidupan saya. Pada 19 Februari 2015, saya menerima kabar buruk bahwa kakek saya telah berpulang ke rumah Tuhan. Kepergian kakek saya sangat membekas di hati banyak orang, terutama nenek saya. Nenek saya sangat merasa kehilangan karena memang nenek belum siap menghadapi hal ini sehingga membuat kondisi badannya melemah. Sejak ditinggal kakek, kondisi mental dan fisik nenek saya semakin memburuk. Awalnya, ia merasa sangat kesepian dan merasa takut jika ditinggal sendirian di rumah. Bahkan, nenek saya sering menangis jika merasa kesepian. Ibu saya dan ketujuh saudara kandungnya akhirnya sepakat untuk bergantian menjaga nenek saya di rumahnya supaya tidak merasa kesepian lagi. Setelah itu, hari-hari nenek saya berjalan normal seperti biasa. Namun, karena umurnya yang bertambah tua, kondisi fisiknya semakin melemah. Sejak 2017, nenek saya sudah tidak kuat lagi berjalan dan harus memakai kursi roda. Di situlah, ketabahan dan kesabaran anak-anaknya, termasuk ibu saya, diuji dalam mengurus nenek saya. Pakde, budhe, tante, dan om saya yang hidup di luar kota, seperti: Jakarta, Yogyakarta, dan Kudus, semakin sering menyempatkan diri pulang ke Salatiga hanya untuk bergiliran mengurus nenek saya. Sampai pada April 2018 lalu, kondisi nenek saya berada di titik terburuknya. Karena anak-anaknya sudah memiliki firasat yang tidak baik, mereka memutuskan untuk berkunjung bersama-sama ke rumah nenek saya. Mereka hanya bisa berdoa bersama untuk kondisi ibu mereka. Sampai pada akhirnya, Tuhan Yesus memanggil nenek saya untuk ikut bersama-Nya. Karena sudah siap dengan kepergian nenek saya, kami semua menerima kepergian nenek dengan sukacita dan penuh ucapan syukur karena nenek saya sudah sembuh dan pergi ke tempat yang lebih indah, menyusul kakek saya. Tidak disangka, kepergian kakek dan nenek saya membawa berkah bagi keluarga besar kami. Tuhan Yesus memiliki kuasa untuk membuat keluarga kami menjadi lebih dekat satu sama lain. Hubungan anak-anak beserta cucu-cucu mereka menjadi lebih dekat. Kakak-kakak Ibu saya yang dahulu sering pulang ke Salatiga hanya untuk bertemu dan menjenguk orang tua mereka, sekarang lebih menghargai waktu kebersamaan dengan keluarga yang diberikan oleh Tuhan. Sejak saat itu, kami semua memiliki satu grup chat dan sering menanyakan kabar satu sama lain. Bahkan, kami semua memiliki keinginan untuk lebih sering bertemu pada masa depan, dan melakukan kegiatan bersama-sama seperti berlibur dan arisan keluarga. Semua itu tidak pernah terjadi sebelum kepergian kakek dan nenek saya, dan saya sungguh percaya Tuhan Yesus turut campur tangan dalam semua kejadian yang menimpa keluarga saya. Ia tidak pernah berhenti untuk menunjukkan betapa sayangnya Ia terhadap anak-anak-Nya, bahkan ketika anak-anak-Nya sedang berada dalam keterpurukan. Tuhan Yesus selalu memiliki rencana yang indah untuk setiap anak-anak-Nya, dan saya sangat percaya Ia telah memberikan sesuatu yang besar untuk membalas rasa kehilangan keluarga saya selama ini. Tuhan Yesus memang sungguh baik! Semoga Tuhan selalu memberkati keluarga Anda!

title: Berbagi dengan Mengajar dan Melayani
title_zh: 通过教学和侍奉来分享
content: Shalom! Perkenalkan nama saya Zefanya. Saya bersyukur karena pada kesempatan ini, saya dapat menyaksikan cinta kasih Tuhan yang Ia nyatakan melalui kegiatan mengajar bahasa Inggris yang saya lakukan secara volunter untuk anak-anak di beberapa desa di sekitar kota Salatiga. Kegiatan yang diselenggarakan oleh salah satu yayasan Kristen yang bergerak di bidang pelayanan dan pendidikan ini dilakukan setiap hari minggu. Pada kesempatan itu, saya beserta teman kuliah dan satu staf dari yayasan mendapat tugas untuk mengajar anak-anak di sebuah desa yang letaknya cukup jauh dari kota Salatiga, tempat kami tinggal. Butuh waktu sekitar dua jam lebih untuk sampai ke sana. Selama perjalanan, medan yang dilalui cukup sulit karena kami harus melewati jalanan aspal yang telah rusak parah dan jalanan tanah yang cukup sempit. Kami juga harus bersahabat dengan hawa panas yang sangat menyengat akibat dari teriknya sinar matahari ditambah dengan banyaknya tanah tandus dan pohon kering di sepanjang perjalanan. Namun, hal tersebut tidak mengurangi semangat kami untuk bertemu dengan anak-anak yang akan kami ajar. Setelah melalui perjalanan yang cukup melelahkan, akhirnya kami tiba di salah satu rumah warga yang akan kami gunakan untuk kegiatan belajar mengajar. Beberapa anak telah berkumpul di dalam rumah itu dan ketika mereka melihat kedatangan kami, mereka langsung membentuk barisan memanjang dan satu per satu mulai memberikan salam kepada kami. Alangkah manisnya! Saya sangat kagum dengan sikap mereka yang sangat ramah yang dapat membuat siapa saja ingin tersenyum ketika melihat mereka. Saya mulai mengajak mereka bercerita tentang pelajaran mereka di sekolah. Ada sekitar dua puluh anak yang datang untuk belajar. Usia mereka bervariasi, dari usia TK hingga SMP. Melalui percakapan mereka, saya mengetahui bahwa sebagian besar dari mereka belum pernah diajarkan bahasa Inggris di sekolah. Anak-anak SMP pun belum mengetahui pelajaran bahasa Inggris tingkat dasar seperti berhitung dari satu hingga sepuluh, atau menulis kosakata sederhana lainnya. Mereka juga bercerita tentang harapan mereka ke depan untuk memiliki fasilitas belajar yang memadai dan memperoleh lebih banyak kesempatan lagi untuk belajar bahasa Inggris. Hal itulah yang membuat kami sadar betapa mereka sangat ingin belajar hal-hal baru, tetapi fasilitas yang ada masih jauh dari kata memadai. Saya pun bersyukur karena dari kegiatan ini, mereka mendapat kesempatan untuk mempelajari hal-hal baru tersebut. Waktu belajar dimulai. Kami mengawalinya dengan berdoa, dan sebagian besar dari mereka, yang berbeda keyakinan, ikut melipat tangan dan menutup mata mereka. Selesai berdoa, kami membagi mereka dalam kelompok kelas kecil dan kelas besar. Kelas kecil terdiri dari anak usia TK hingga kelas tiga SD, sedangkan kelas besar terdiri dari anak-anak kelas empat SD ke atas. Saya mendapat kesempatan untuk mengajar anak-anak kelas besar. Banyak hal yang saya coba ajarkan kepada mereka, mulai dari kosakata sederhana tentang binatang, mengerjakan soal, hingga bermain gim sederhana untuk mengasah kemampuan bahasa Inggris mereka. Rasa lelah dan capai tentu kami rasakan karena mengajar anak-anak seusia mereka bukanlah perkara yang mudah. Namun, pada saat seperti itulah, kami menyadari bahwa kegiatan tersebut kami lakukan untuk memuliakan nama Tuhan. Kami yakin dan percaya bahwa Tuhanlah yang akan memberi kekuatan yang membuat kami mampu untuk melakukannya dengan baik. Kegiatan hari itupun selesai. Kami bersyukur bahwa kegiatan mengajar itu dapat kami lakukan dengan cukup baik terlepas dari kekurangan dan kendala yang kami rasakan sewaktu mengajar. Semangat belajar dari anak-anak juga membuat kami terdorong untuk memberikan pengajaran yang lebih baik lagi pada masa yang akan datang. Kami sangat bersyukur karena Tuhan memberikan perlindungan dan kasih-Nya kepada anak-anak yang kami ajar sehingga mereka masih dapat bertumbuh dengan baik dan memperoleh kesempatan-kesempatan untuk mengembangkan pengetahuan mereka.
