content: The word epiphany is defined by the Oxford Learner’s Dictionary as “a sudden and surprising moment of understanding.” Often, such epiphany moments arrive unexpectedly, interrupting the ordinary rhythms of life with extraordinary insight. Sometimes they come through a conversation, a passage of Scripture, or an encounter with nature. Other times, they emerge through art. Twilight Epiphany. Photo: Eliott Davis Sitting beneath artist James Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany on the campus of Rice University in Houston, Texas, on a Sunday morning as the sun rose, the word epiphany took on new meaning. As the morning light slowly illuminated the sky, subtle shifts in color transformed the space above me. The experience was both architectural and atmospheric, a convergence of art, nature, and contemplation. Turrell, born in 1943, is an American artist internationally recognized for his exploration of light, space, and human perception. Raised in the Quaker tradition, Turrell’s artistic vision reflects an appreciation for silence, stillness, and inward reflection. Commissioned by Rice University through the generosity of alumna Suzanne Deal Booth, Twilight Epiphany opened in 2012 as part of the university’s public art program. The pyramidal Skyspace, designed to accommodate approximately 120 visitors, features an aperture in its roof through which viewers observe the changing sky. At sunrise and sunset, carefully programmed LED lights interact with the natural atmosphere, creating an extraordinary experience of shifting color and perception. More than a work of architecture, the installation invites visitors to slow down, look upward, and reconsider the relationship between light and the world around them. James Turrell (Chat GPT) For me, the experience was something of a spiritual exercise. Light, after all, is among the Bible’s most enduring metaphors for divine revelation, truth, and beauty. As the colors shifted above me, I was reminded that beauty does not always announce itself loudly. Sometimes it simply asks us to be still and pay attention. Rothko Chapel. Photo: https://www.mark-rothko.org/rothko-chapel.jsp#google_vignette. From Rice University, I headed to another meditative landmark: the Rothko Chapel . Here, I sat among the monumental, dark-hued paintings of Mark Rothko, contemplating both the tragedy of the artist’s life and the triumph of the chapel that bears his name. Commissioned by Houston philanthropists John and Dominique de Menil in 1964 and dedicated in 1971, the Rothko Chapel is an interfaith sanctuary devoted to contemplation, spiritual reflection, and human rights. Its octagonal interior contains fourteen large-scale paintings by Rothko, whose subtle variations of black, maroon, and purple create an atmosphere of profound stillness. Rothko, born Marcus Rothkowitz in 1903, was a leading figure in American Abstract Expressionism, celebrated for his ability to evoke deep emotional responses through color and form. Yet his personal life was marked by physical illness, depression, and emotional turmoil. In February 1970, before the chapel’s dedication, Rothko died by suicide at the age of sixty-six. He never witnessed the completed sanctuary that would become one of his most enduring artistic legacies. Twilight Epiphany. Photo: Brian C. Nixon There is something deeply moving about this juxtaposition. An artist whose life ended in despair left behind a place where countless visitors have sought peace, meaning, and solace. The darkness of Rothko’s paintings does not necessarily communicate hopelessness. Rather, their quiet intensity invites viewers to confront the depths of human experience—sorrow, longing, mystery, and perhaps even transcendence. Where Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany draws the eyes upward toward the heavens, Rothko’s chapel seems to draw the gaze inward, toward the mysteries of the human soul. One is animated by the changing light of the sky, the other by the stillness of darkened canvases. Yet both offer some

summary: While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.” From Montgomery’s framed correspondence […]  The post  Lanier’s Sixth Annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series: A Grand Success  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: John Warwick Montgomery While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.” From Montgomery’s framed correspondence with C. S. Lewis and his barrister gowns to the thousands of books that comprise his remarkable personal collection, Lanier has provided the Christian world with a marvelous tribute to one of the great Christian intellectuals of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Born in 1931, John Warwick Montgomery (d. 2024) was a distinguished Christian apologist, theologian, attorney, and scholar whose extraordinary career spanned several disciplines. Holding numerous academic degrees, including doctorates in theology, philosophy, and law, Montgomery became internationally recognized for his defense of Christianity through historical evidence, legal reasoning, and philosophical argumentation. His influential books, including History and Christianity , Faith Founded on Fact , and The Shape of the Past , helped establish a rigorous approach to Christian apologetics. Whether lecturing in universities, debating skeptics, or practicing law, Montgomery maintained that Christianity was not merely a matter of subjective belief but a faith grounded in historical reality and rational inquiry. Yet to stop at the library would be to understate Lanier’s remarkable work. The sixth annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series was a tour de force of distinguished thinkers, passionate Christians, and intellectually engaging presentations. More than a commemoration of Montgomery’s life, the gathering represented a continuation of his intellectual legacy: the conviction that Christianity can withstand serious scrutiny and offer compelling answers to life’s most profound questions. Mark Lanier, Nancy Pearcey, Paul Gould, Adam Francisco, and Michael Horton From the opening panel discussion hosted by attorney and philanthropist Mark Lanier to Dr. Paul Gould’s thoughtful presentation on worldviews, followed by attorney Craig Parton’s lecture on jurisprudential apologetics, one theme emerged with unmistakable clarity: Christianity is a reasonable faith. The presentations reflected Montgomery’s own interdisciplinary approach to apologetics: the Christian faith and intellectual inquiry need not be adversaries. Indeed, the Christian tradition has long insisted that faith and reason are complementary avenues in the pursuit of truth. The following day continued this rich intellectual exploration. Professor Nancy Pearcey addressed questions surrounding truth, dismantling various modern ideologies, while Dr. Adam Francisco offered an informative overview of Islamic history and belief, helping participants better understand one of world’s biggest religions. The keynote address by Dr. Michael Horton examined the challenge of reaching those who identify as “spiritual but not religious,” a growing segment of contemporary society. Horton’s presentation underscored the importance of communicating historic Christian truth in a culture increasingly suspicious of religious institutions yet often deeply interested in spiritual meaning. Dr. Michael Horton On Sunday morning, Lanier founder, Mark Lanier, hosted many participants during his Biblical literacy class, where he continued the dialogue with Michael Horton. Taken together, the lectures, discussions, and interviews demonstrated the breadth of Christian scholarship and the continuing relevance of thoughtful apologetics in an age of skepticism, religious pluralism, and cultural uncertainty. content: What do Jesus and Isaiah have in common? Quite a bit, according to renowned British New Testament scholar N. T. Wright. Gathering at the marvelous Lanier Theological Library in Houston, Texas—the brainchild of noted attorney, author, and biblical scholar Mark Lanier—Wright offered a packed house in the Great Room a fascinating glimpse into the relationship between the Old Testament prophet Isaiah and the life, ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Dr. Joseph Holden of Veritas International University listening to Dr. NT Wright at Lanier Library. For Wright, Isaiah is far more than an ancient prophetic voice whose words occasionally appear in the New Testament. Rather, the prophet provides a theological framework for understanding Jesus and the unfolding purposes of God. In his book Into the Heart of Isaiah , Wright invites readers to rediscover the extraordinary depth of Isaiah’s prophetic vision, demonstrating how its themes of judgment, restoration, redemption, and new creation find their ultimate expression in Christ. Central to Wright’s interpretation is the conviction that Isaiah’s message cannot be separated from the larger story of Israel. The prophet speaks of exile and homecoming, divine judgment and covenant faithfulness, suffering and salvation. These themes, Wright argues, become essential to understanding how Jesus understood his own mission and how the earliest Christians interpreted his life. Particularly significant is Isaiah’s portrayal of the suffering servant, whose affliction becomes the means through which God’s redemptive purposes are accomplished. Wright connects this prophetic imagery to Jesus’ sacrificial death, while emphasizing that the cross cannot be isolated from the broader biblical promise of God’s restoration of creation. Equally important is Isaiah’s vision of a renewed world, a creation in which justice, righteousness, and peace flourish under God’s reign. For Wright, the resurrection of Jesus announces the beginning of that promised new creation. The Christian hope, therefore, is not simply an escape from the present world, but the ultimate renewal of God’s good creation. Personal Stories: Mounting Up with Wings Like Eagles Amid the theological insights and biblical exposition, Wright shared several personal stories, offering the audience a glimpse into how the words of Isaiah have shaped not only his scholarship but also his spiritual imagination. One story centered on the beloved passage from Isaiah 40:31, in which the prophet declares that those who wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles. Wright recalled preaching on Isaiah many years earlier and drew an amusing comparison to the long-running British radio program Desert Island Discs , in which notable guests select the recordings they would take with them if stranded on a deserted island. “I’ve sometimes said I have a set of desert island texts,” Wright explained, suggesting that certain biblical passages remain especially meaningful throughout one’s life. Near the top of his list, he said, is the closing portion of Isaiah 40, with its magnificent image of soaring eagles. The passage, he suggested, is more than a favorite theological text. It is part of his personal testimony, a biblical promise that has accompanied him through the years. A second story brought the imagery of Isaiah into an unexpected encounter with the natural world. While completing the final proofreading of Into the Heart of Isaiah , Wright and his wife, Maggie, were staying at their home in Scotland. Wright was alone in a room, carefully reviewing the text, when something outside caught his attention. “Out of the corner of my eye, I saw something,” he recalled. “At first, I thought it was somebody’s dog that had come into our front garden.” Noted Biblical archeologist, Dr. Steven Collins, listening to Mark Lanier interview Dr. NT Wright at Lanier Library. content: By Charles Gardner — When a Japanese sailor’s destroyer was sunk by the Americans in a World War II South Pacific battle, most of his companions drowned. Amazingly, even though he was sucked underneath the waves with others as the ship went down, torpedo officer Michiharu Shinya somehow survived this 1942 disaster. (Only 18 of the 200-strong crew did). But he would rather have died at that point as his people had been indoctrinated to believe that it was shameful to be captured. Nevertheless, he was badly wounded but nursed back to health by medics. In time, he was picked up and eventually taken to a Prisoner-of-War camp at Featherston, near Wellington, in New Zealand, where he was to spend the next three years, as Don Stephens records in his inspirational book War and Grace (Evangelical Press, an imprint of 10Publishing). Shinya and his fellow inmates were treated with much kindness (in sharp contrast to the torture often experienced by Allied prisoners at the hands of the Japanese). Being showered with gifts at Christmas, a feast he knew nothing about, seemed especially strange. However, he was determined not to be ‘taken in’ by the Christian teaching offered after some of the prisoners requested spiritual help and a Japanese Bible was made available. That is until he chanced upon an article entitled ‘Sorrow in Victory’ in which the author quoted a ‘Hebrew prophet’ as saying: “Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength. They shall soar on wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not be faint.” It made a deep impression on him, and he was determined to find out where it came from. Assuming it was from the Old Testament, he began reading the Bible, starting at Genesis chapter 1. Eventually, to his joy, he discovered that the profound words were from the Book of the prophet Isaiah (chapter 40, verse 31). After flagging somewhat in his search, he found himself hospitalised with malaria when a friend brought him a booklet called The Reason Why explaining the way to salvation. It so happened that the camp’s chaplain, Pastor Hessell Troughton, had been a missionary to Japan and spoke the language. Shinya joined others in his Bible studies and came to know and love Jesus as his Saviour. So much did this “complete freedom” now rule his life that prison had morphed into what he described as “a unique paradise on earth”. He never looked back after that and became convinced that his post-war calling would be in service of his Lord. When he finally returned home, his family were shocked to see him alive for he had been reported as killed in action. He had also given a false name to his captors because of the supposed shame of falling into enemy hands. Shinya subsequently became a pastor and prolific writer and translator following years of theological study both in Tokyo and the US. The Old Testament, he came to believe, demonstrated that sin is “the ultimate problem of mankind” and clearly pointed to Christ as the answer. On seeking to understand why so few Japanese became Christians, he felt it was partly due to their pride borne of believing they were a superior race. As for those three Christmases he spent in New Zealand, author Don Stephens writes: “Of all the gifts he received, the one he valued most was ‘the boundless and deep grace and peace of God in the Lord Jesus Christ’.” The post WWII Japanese POW found ‘freedom’ in camp first appeared on God Reports .

title: In the shadow of western stars: Grover Lewis, Larry McMurtry, and the triumph of words
summary: With The Grover Lewis Reader: Splendor in the Short Grass and Western Star, the newest biography of Larry McMurtry, in hand, I load my truck and head toward Archer City, Texas, accompanied by my wife, Melanie, and our friend Eliott. Archer City is, of course, McMurtry country, a small Texas town made famous through the literary imagination of […]  The post  In the shadow of western stars: Grover Lewis, Larry McMurtry, and the triumph of words  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: With The Grover Lewis Reader: Splendor in the Short Grass and Western Star , the newest biography of Larry McMurtry, in hand, I load my truck and head toward Archer City, Texas, accompanied by my wife, Melanie, and our friend Eliott. Archer City is, of course, McMurtry country, a small Texas town made famous through the literary imagination of one of America’s most celebrated novelists. Having written about McMurtry’s faith—or lack thereof—in a previous article , following an earlier visit to Archer City, I’m returning with a somewhat different interest. This time, my attention turns to Grover Lewis, the gifted journalist, critic, and poet whose life intersected with McMurtry’s during their college years. Lewis’ story, however, begins not with literary achievement but with almost unimaginable tragedy. As a child, he experienced the devastating loss of both parents when his father murdered his mother and was subsequently shot with the same gun, either by his dying wife or another person present. Lewis was only eight years old. It is difficult to imagine a more horrific beginning. Yet rather than allowing that tragedy to become the entirety of his story, Lewis eventually found a voice through literature. Perhaps the cards life dealt him gave him plenty to write about. Or perhaps writing became his way of making sense of a world that had revealed its cruelty far too early. In his autobiographical poem “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis writes: “You asked me once, Ann/Over coffee gone cold with talk/In your mother’s rain-drowsy/House, who they were, how it/Was with them in their breathless/Time in the wilds of years.” For Lewis, those early years were indeed wild. But they were also the soil from which his literary imagination would eventually grow. A Life in Words Born in Texas in 1934, Grover Lewis emerged as a distinctive voice in American journalism, particularly through his cultural criticism and reporting on the rapidly changing landscape of the 1960s and 1970s. He became known for his sharp observations, literary flair, and ability to capture the personalities and contradictions of American culture, even if he occasionally stretched the truth in the telling. His work appeared in prominent publications, including Rolling Stone , where his reporting helped establish his reputation as an insightful, sometimes cutting observer of popular culture. Lewis was more than a journalist, however. He was a poet and literary craftsman, someone who understood that words could do more than convey information. They could illuminate the human condition, expose its contradictions, and perhaps even provide a measure of healing. Grover Lewis (ChatPGT) Continuing “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis ponders: “At last, breathless and dry-mouthed/With private desire in the blue,/Swollen dark, we all lie down together—/My mother, my father, their perishing/Dreams, and I this unborn prisoner son…” There is something haunting about these lines. The dead remain present. The past refuses to disappear. And the poet, even as an adult, seems to wrestle with the circumstances that shaped his entrance into the world. Yet the very act of writing suggests something else: a refusal to remain silent. Two Texans, Two Literary Paths Lewis and Larry McMurtry crossed paths as students at North Texas State College, now the University of North Texas, during the 1950s. Both were young Texans drawn to literature and the possibilities of the written word. Their friendship developed within a shared intellectual environment, one that encouraged reading, conversation, and the pursuit of literary ambitions. Although their careers eventually followed different paths—McMurtry toward novels, screenplays, and literary fame, Lewis toward journalism, poetry, and cultural criticism—they shared an interest in the complexities of American life. content: Pastor Peter Colon portraying Major Rossvally in the movie of his story By Charles Gardner — A Jewish army surgeon was amazed by the courage of a young soldier badly wounded in the Battle of Gettysburg during the American Civil War (1861-65). Dr Max Rossvally was forced to amputate both a leg and arm in a bid to save the boy’s life. But it changed his own life. For the 17-year-old Drummer Boy – too young for frontline duty – refused chloroform or brandy to dull the pain. Charlie Coulson chose instead to trust in Jesus, his Lord and Saviour. The doctor – an army major and Orthodox Jew – was understandably stunned by the boy’s bravery, as well as his boldness in declaring his faith in Christ and imploring the officer (whom he knew to be Jewish) to put his own trust in Jesus, since he was also the Jewish Messiah. Max, however, was shaken rigid, and in a great dilemma, as he had always been taught to hate Jesus. For his people had largely rejected him as an ‘impostor’ and false Messiah. Charlie died just days later, apparently more concerned for the doctor’s eternal destiny than for his own painful exit from this life. Ten years later, Max found himself in a barber’s chair in New York once more being urged to trust in Jesus. Having explained the gospel, the barber promised to pray for him and said that, whenever he came in contact with a Jew, he felt it his duty to introduce him to the one who came for “the lost sheep of Israel” (Matthew 10:6). The surgeon subsequently boarded a train for a business meeting in Washington, where a newspaper advertisement drew him to a ‘revival’ service where the preacher echoed the messages he had heard from the barber and the boy soldier, leaving him in tears. He agonised at home in prayer for some time afterwards, struggling most of all with the thought that, if he accepted Christ, he would be going against all the advice and teaching he had known, not to mention the Jewish community as a whole. But he finally became convinced that Jesus was indeed the fulfilment of Old Testament prophecies (in particular, Genesis 49:10, Micah 5:2 and Isaiah 7:14). So he prayed: “O Lord God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. You know I am sincere in this thing. If Jesus Christ is the Son of God, reveal him to me this night, and I will accept him as my Messiah.” A long battle ensued, but his doubts were eventually replaced by joy and happiness as he praised God that he had found the true Shiloh, Ruler of Israel and Emmanuel. He was to pay a high price, however, as do all who follow Christ. His wife walked out on him; his parents disowned him. But he never gave up hope as he constantly prayed and reached out to his family. After 54 days, his wife joined him as a disciple of Jesus and, in time, his daughter also became a believer. But his son disowned him for many years until he was eventually reconciled both with his earthly and heavenly Father. In an extraordinary sequel some 18 months after he came to Christ, Max met up with Mrs Coulson, the mother of his dying young patient all those years earlier on the battlefield. With great joy, he was able to share how her son had set him on the path to a glorious future in Christ, which was to touch lives across the world, including my home county of Yorkshire in England. In fact, he came to live in Leeds to reach out to the Jewish community there and is buried at Lawnswood Cemetery in the city. An Irish friend of mine, Colin Nevin, has visited the grave, which includes an excerpt from one of the doctor’s hymns, I am Coming Soon, and was able to give a copy of Max’s story to a caretaker, so continuing the evangelist’s legacy more than a century after his death in 1892, aged 64. A 54-minute movie – Rossvally: From the Synagogue to the Saviour – has been produced on DVD and can apparently be ordered online. content: By Charles Gardner — We used to be regular viewers of the The Great British Bake-Off TV series, now being screened on Channel 4, celebrating the efforts of amateur contestants in the kitchen. My wife is qualified in home economics and once, in her far-off student days, helped Mary Berry out over the weekend. I too like to lend a hand with my cooking skills. So when, the other day, we were intrigued to see how new presenter Nigella Lawson was doing on the show, we switched it on – and were truly appalled at the foul language spewing out of the mouths of at least two contestants. Taking the name of the Lord Jesus Christ in vain, they loudly expressed their frustration (rather than praise) at things going wrong with their concoctions in front of more than seven million viewers. We switched it off, vowing to complain in the strongest possible terms, which I have since done. And though it’s hard to be surprised at the language regularly heard on television programmes these days, I was shocked to the core by Channel 4’s response, basically saying that this particularly offensive blasphemy doesn’t come under the category of “strong language”. Really? It’s surely the worst of them all. “We are sorry to hear you were offended by some of the language used within the programme,” they wrote. “Whilst we do appreciate that you find the use of such phrases or words unacceptable, we are not obliged under the Ofcom code to obscure them, nor do they fall under the category for strong language. We therefore have no obligation to bleep them either pre- or post-watershed.” I had suggested that they could at least have edited them out, adding that they were being very hypocritical as they wouldn’t have allowed swearing in the name of Mohammed, a point which they ignored. Have we sunk so low in our nation that there is nothing left that is sacred, except woke left-wing ideology and appeasement of those who hate the God of Israel and his Son Jesus, our Lord? But we have forsaken the God who brought peace and prosperity to Britain, and who saved us from Nazi invasion, for the idols of food and celebrity. Shame on us! Is it not time the Christian world woke up and stood against this flood of filth in our midst, which will sweep us away into the oblivion of a third-rate country if we do not act soon. Where has the ‘land of hope and glory’ gone? The ‘mother of the free’ we sing about at the Proms, calling on the God ‘who made thee mighty’ to ‘make thee mightier yet’? The Apostle Paul was surely prophesying the decline and fall of the Roman Empire in his letter to the early Christians in Rome (a mixture of Jews and Gentiles), when he wrote: “The wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of men who suppress the truth by their wickedness, since what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them. For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities – his eternal power and divine nature – have been clearly seen, being understood from what has been made, so that men are without excuse.” (Romans 1:18-20) The post Offended by foul language on food show first appeared on God Reports .

content: By Mike Shreve — Tent meeting in the 80s Evangelism has been my focus for 55 years, ministering throughout the United States and in 14 other nations. God mercifully saved me during the Jesus Revolution (1970), out of a hippie lifestyle and a passionate, though misguided pursuit of truth through far eastern religious practices (yoga and meditation). Shortly after encountering Jesus and being delivered, along with another brother in the Lord, I began hitchhiking around the country, preaching the Gospel on street corners and college campuses. That developed through the years into ministry in churches, auditoriums, conferences, and tent crusades. Supernatural provision and divine intervention has always carried me, through every phase of this five-and-a-half-decade-long adventure. However, the following story is a classic. For about 25 years I carried big Gospel tents around the country. At the time of this “miracle,” I was transporting a 60’ x 90’ tent from one city to the next in an old, dilapidated bus that kept introducing new challenges to our amateur mechanic skills (putting it mildly). One day, on our way to Tampa, Florida—unfortunately—we hit a large pothole in the road that put a serious dent in the rear left rim on which a large truck tire was mounted. From that point, the inner tube would not retain air, making it necessary to stop every thirty miles or so to fill it up again . . . and again . . . and again . . . making the trip painfully slow. Adding to the problem, the other rear tire was bald, and we had no spare (couldn’t afford one). So, a flat would have brought us to a complete standstill. Sometimes, I think back on those days (when our zeal for the Kingdom outran any wisdom we might have possessed), and I marvel at the many times God took care of us anyway (like the loving heavenly Father that He is). Thousands of pounds of equipment were packed into that groaning, creaking, rusty, decrepit bus — heavy canvas tent sections, metal poles, stakes, platform, and 300 chairs—and only a few days allowed in between cities for transit and setup. No, we really could not afford any setbacks. And yes, a lot of “faith prayers” were uttered during every trip (or were they “presumptive proclamations”—not sure—maybe a mix of the two). An old split rim tire mounted on an old bus Once we got to Tampa, attempting to be frugal, I visited the junkyards hoping to find a used replacement rim. As if they had conspired to dissuade me, every junkyard owner/manager shot down my hopes with a similar assessment, “Fella, you won’t find one of them old split-rims anywhere. They’re dangerous. When you try to mount a tire on one, they can snap open and injure somebody real bad, cutting off a hand, even killing a person. We melted ‘em all down as scrap metal.” (Go ahead, look them up online—they were even called “widow-makers.”) It was the same story everywhere I went. Nobody could help. Then three weeks passed and we had to pack the bus and head to our next location—Bessemer City, North Carolina. It was a college-level, biblically-sound course on developing long-suffering and patience: stopping every thirty miles or so to air up that unpredictable tire, pleading with God to somehow supernaturally assist us in our journey by making sure none of the tires blew. Somehow, we made it—around 600 miles—stopping about 25 times. Then an incredible miracle happened! God did it and I still feel awestruck, just writing about it. As we turned into the fairgrounds area, right in the middle of the entrance were two brand new, neatly-stacked truck tires (unclaimed), exactly the size we used on the bus—mounted (you guessed it!) on the very same split rims our bus required. Talk about worshiping God—we launched into a praise session right then and there! What were the odds? We all knew it had to be God. content: By Charles Gardner — Barrie Clark painting of a Spitfire The Battle of Britain, which saw Spitfires and Hurricanes save us from Nazi invasion and ensure our freedom, apparently ended after three months on October 31, 1940. As we move past that date this year, many of us will no doubt be distracted by superficial celebrations like Halloween, more animated by the spectre of ghosts and witches than the real threats to our society from those who would rob us of our hard-fought freedom. Our present government would have us paralyzed with fear and trepidation as they urge us to stock up our cupboards in case of emergency, but Jesus reminds us how he takes care of the sparrows and urges us to trust him for all our needs. That wartime battle in the skies would not have been won without a nationwide turning to God in prayer, and the current challenges can only be overcome in the spiritual realm. For there is a ferocious war taking place in the heavenly places (see Ephesians 6:12) urgently requiring our participation. My Uncle Murray flew both planes mentioned above as an RAF Wing Commander during the war, and I have a painting of a Spitfire above my desk as a constant reminder of the spiritual battle we face. Tragically, an increasing section of our society are taken in by the lying propaganda of Hamas and their fellow travelers, with a jihadist agenda to rid the world of the Jewish people who brought Western civilization to the fore. The Nazi invasion we managed to prevent has come in another guise. All of which means there’s a furious battle for the soul of Britain for which we need spiritual ‘fighter pilots’ to prayerfully shoot down the archenemies of our once Christian nation by standing up for the truth Jesus came to bring us. Meanwhile left-wing activists supposedly supporting the Palestinian cause have engaged in cowardly vandalism of properties reputedly belonging to employees of companies selling military equipment to Israel. And during an anti-Israel protest in London on October 17 the Battle of Britain monument was attacked by pro-Palestinian protesters who smashed poppy wreaths dedicated to those brave men who gave their all defending our freedom. One woman was arrested after she was seen giving a Nazi salute! All these sentiments are being fuelled by our own government’s attitudes to Israel and by their cowardice in pandering to the prejudice of those whose votes they covet. But praise God for those ten thousand who have taken the trouble to sign a Christians United For Israel petition opposing sanctions on Israel. Western civilization is under serious threat. Israel is fighting to preserve Western civilization, and at a frontier the West prefers not to name: Islamic extremism and its call for global political control.” If the West rewards the October 7th, 2023, massacre with political gains, like the ‘state’ of Palestine in the midst of Israel, “it teaches a lesson to every violent movement on earth: that massacre pays”. title: Rejoice in the Lamb: Benjamin Britten, Christopher Smart, and the Poetry of Faith
summary: When music meets poetry, the result can be more than art, it can become an expression of spiritual wonder. The last time I heard Professor Bruce Redford speak about the eccentric British clergyman and poet Christopher Smart (1722–1771), I was so inspired that I included a substantial portion of Smart’s extraordinary poem, Jubilate Agno, in […]  The post  Rejoice in the Lamb: Benjamin Britten, Christopher Smart, and the Poetry of Faith  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: When music meets poetry, the result can be more than art, it can become an expression of spiritual wonder. Christopher Smart The last time I heard Professor Bruce Redford speak about the eccentric British clergyman and poet Christopher Smart (1722–1771), I was so inspired that I included a substantial portion of Smart’s extraordinary poem, Jubilate Agno , in my book Beauty (And the Banana) . I described Smart as a theopoet , someone whose deep religious convictions found expression through a distinctive and imaginative poetic vision. Smart was no ordinary poet. His writings moved freely between the sacred and the seemingly mundane, finding divine significance in everything from biblical figures to animals and the natural world. His poetry was exuberant, unconventional, and, at times, wonderfully strange. For Smart, creation itself was a chorus of praise, and every living thing had a part to play. Recently, I had another opportunity to hear Redford explore Smart’s remarkable literary legacy, this time through the music of British composer Benjamin Britten (1913–1976). As part of an All Saints’ Day concert at the Cathedral of St. John in Albuquerque, New Mexico, celebrating Britten’s music, Redford delivered a pre-concert lecture focusing on the composer’s Rejoice in the Lamb , a choral masterpiece that brings Smart’s unusual poetry to life. The evening offered a fascinating intersection of literature, music, theology, and history, demonstrating how two artists separated by nearly two centuries could share a common vision of wonder. The Musical Imagination of Benjamin Britten Benjamin Britten. Photo: Public Domain. Redford, a former professor at Boston University who was living in England when Britten died in 1976, identified three defining characteristics of the composer’s work. First, Britten’s music is distinguished by “passion and variety.” His compositions resist easy categorization, moving between emotional intensity, dramatic storytelling, and moments of remarkable spiritual intimacy. Redford described Britten’s approach as creating a kind of musical parable, pointing to Curlew River , one of Britten’s church parables, as a particularly compelling example. Second, Britten demonstrated an extraordinary ability to balance “economy and scope.” Redford compared this quality to the novels of Jane Austen, whose carefully constructed narratives reveal entire worlds through seemingly modest details. Similarly, Britten could communicate profound emotional and spiritual truths through restrained musical means. Nothing was wasted; every note served a purpose. Third, and perhaps most important for the evening’s performance, Britten possessed an exceptional “sensitivity to words.” Redford described him as an “inspired” interpreter of literary texts, a composer who understood that music should not merely accompany poetry but illuminate its deeper meaning. It was this third characteristic that led Redford to Christopher Smart. When an Eccentric Poet Meets a Brilliant Composer In 1943, Britten composed Rejoice in the Lamb (Op. 30), a festival cantata scored for four soloists, SATB choir, and organ. The composition draws its text from Smart’s Jubilate Agno , a work of religious poetry that remained largely unknown for nearly two centuries. Christopher Smart Smart wrote much of the poem during his confinement in a private madhouse in eighteenth-century London. Its unconventional structure, biblical references, exuberant language, and seemingly spontaneous declarations of praise made it unlike almost anything else in English religious literature. The manuscript remained unpublished until W. F. Stead brought it to public attention in 1939. Soon afterward, the poet W. H. Auden introduced Britten to Smart’s newly published work while the composer was living in the United States. The connection proved fruitful. Britten recognized something remarkable in Smart’s poetry: an unrestrained celebration of creation that could be translated into music.

title: Iran hangs over Israel’s election like ghastly Halloween ghost
summary: By Charles Gardner — The watching world is holding its breath after record numbers of Israelis went to the polls. content: By Charles Gardner — The watching world is holding its breath after record numbers of Israelis went to the polls. We perhaps need reminding that the Jewish state is the only democracy in the Middle East and has been on an almost constant war-footing since the last national elections four years ago. With all the regular ballots counted, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc leads that of ex-military chief Gadi Eisenkot by 53-48 seats, with the Arab parties winning the remaining 19. That leaves the incumbent needing to persuade eight Arab members to make up the required 61-seat Knesset majority by joining him in a coalition. Negotiations are expected to take some time. Modern Israel has been under threat ever since her re-birth in 1948, but the situation is worse than ever since the Hamas massacre of October 7, 2023 – the most severe attack on Jews since the Holocaust. As with Lebanon-based Hezbollah, the Hamas terrorists are backed by Iran, which has long vowed to wipe Israel off the map and is now reportedly very close to nuclear capability. All of which explains why the spectre of Iran hangs over the election like a ghastly Halloween ghost. ‘Bibi’ Netanyahu has even created an AI-generated image of Tel Aviv being struck by an atomic bomb. The nuclear threat is real, and the mullahs would love to vaporise the city’s large Jewish population (which includes many peace-loving Arabs). Netanyahu – who has led the country on and off for the past 30 years – is a firm and steady figure who can be relied upon to defend his country to the death, whereas some opposition candidates could be more accommodating to the demands of Western leaders for two-state solutions, though I doubt they will go that far as a Palestinian state in the midst of Israel is seen by many as signing a death warrant. However, former PM Ariel Sharon (another ex-military chief) effectively gave away Gaza in 2005 in a so-called ‘land for peace’ deal. And how did Gaza thank Israel? With constant attacks on their generous neighbours! In a nation surrounded by enemies, defence is obviously a major factor in policy making, but the irony is that military men (like Sharon) don’t always see things as clearly as the political sharpshooters. President Trump backs Netanyahu because “there’s a job to finish”, but Israel cannot afford to keep relying on allies, including America. Significantly, Bibi is a friend of evangelical Christians, repeatedly acknowledging their unstinting support while the world increasingly turns against them. This support is borne of biblical understanding of God’s long-term purposes for Israel who are not just fighting for their own survival. For the future of the West itself is at stake if we allow Islamic jihadism to win the day in the Middle East. After all, democracy emerged from our understanding of the Bible which in turn came to us from the Jewish prophets, Jesus himself being the cornerstone. It’s not for nothing that our Parliament’s floor is inscribed with the (Latin) words of Psalm 127:1 – “Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labour in vain.” Bibi, for one, is a Bible-believer. That is, he believes the Tenach (our Old Testament) is divinely authored, having repeatedly stated that Israel is a fulfilment of Ezekiel’s prophecy of the Valley of Dry Bones turning into a latter-day resurrection. Legendary Baptist minister Charles Spurgeon also said as much in a sermon over 150 years ago. Evangelicals, who also believe in the Bible’s divine inspiration, are surely called to support Israel, though not uncritically, but in recognising God’s everlasting love for her (Jeremiah 31:3) along with his promise of spiritual restoration. Whatever the outcome of this election, failing to bless Israel will invite a curse on us and our nation (Genesis 12:3). title: Jewish refugee became vicar
summary: By Charles Gardner — At a time when Hitler aimed to harm us, here was a German who came to bless us! Holocaust survivor Werner Simonson escaped from Germany just before the outbreak of World War II, only to become a Church of England vicar. Of Jewish heritage, he was sacked as a judge by […]  The post  Jewish refugee became vicar  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: Werner Simonson By Charles Gardner — At a time when Hitler aimed to harm us, here was a German who came to bless us! Holocaust survivor Werner Simonson escaped from Germany just before the outbreak of World War II, only to become a Church of England vicar. Of Jewish heritage, he was sacked as a judge by the Nazis and had to endure long years of separation from his non-Jewish wife and son before being reunited after the war. Like John Wesley who was rescued as a child from a rectory fire, Werner was also ‘a brand plucked from the burning’. He was about to be executed in a World War I battle with France when he and his colleagues were wrongly accused of shooting French prisoners. But just in time, one of the latter told the firing squad how Werner had treated him with kindness, even sharing his rations with him. The German soldier was thus spared but spent the next five years as a prisoner of the French, his POW status only ending in 1920 after being put to work restoring war damage in northern France. When finally released, it was a case of ‘from the frying pan into the fire’ as Germany was plunged into despair and division following their ignominious defeat. Despite this, however, Werner quickly rose to the status of high court judge before being dismissed from his post by the Nazis when they discovered his Jewish heritage. The fact that he had fought for Germany and had won the coveted Iron Cross for gallantry counted for nothing. And the increasing pressure of anticipating arrest led to a breakdown of his health. But while attending his niece’s confirmation at a Lutheran church, feeling at the end of his rope, it was as if the preacher was speaking directly into his desperate situation. He opened his heart to Christ and found new life and hope. “In the utter darkness which had engulfed my life I saw a new light,” he recalled.(1) He became associated with the Confessing Church opposing the Nazis’ antisemitic policies and was advised to escape which he managed to do with the help of the Bishop of Chichester Dr George Bell. Werner’s wife Leonie and son Juergen stayed behind but were able to join him after the war. Being German, he was initially interned with others on the Isle of Man where he led fellow Jews to faith in Christ. But tragic news followed, hearing of his father’s death, his mother being murdered in a concentration camp and his sister Ilse gassed in Auschwitz. Werner knew little English when he arrived on these shores but attracted much interest by being ordained at St Paul’s Cathedral when Britain was in the middle of a war with his fatherland. He was subsequently offered back the post of judge in the new West Germany along with a pension for the job from which he had been previously dismissed by the Nazis. But he turned down the generous offer. “I could not exchange service in the ministry of God for service in administering man-made law; accepting this offer would have meant abandoning God’s call to me, and this I could not do.” But this humble and self-effacing man was to make a significant impact in succeeding years as he proclaimed the gospel in three separate London parishes, ending up at St Luke’s, Hampstead, where (from 1956-1965) he helped yet more Jewish people to a knowledge of their Messiah. He continued passionately preaching Christ almost till his final breath in 1991, aged 101. 1 With grateful thanks to War and Grace by Don Stephens (Evangelical Press 2005), an imprint of 10Publishing. content: By Mark Ellis – As a 10-year-old boy, Mark Davidson’s mother gave him Hal Lindsey’s book, The Late Great Planet Earth , which eventually sold some 35 million copies, and was declared the bestselling nonfiction book of the 1970s by the New York Times. The book had a great impact on Davidson and shaped his earliest views about end times Bible prophecy. Shaken by the events of 9/11, Davidson, a retired aerospace engineer, dug more deeply into end-times prophecy, seeking answers about the direction of world events.  As he dove into Scripture related to prophecy, he developed a framework that diverges from traditional teaching in several ways, and resulted in his book: Daniel Revisited : Discovering the Four Mideast Signs Leading to the Antichrist. The most relevant of his teaching to current events is his view of Iran. Based on his study of Daniel 7, Daniel 8 and Revelation 6, Davidson identified four major events, which he calls “signposts,” that he believes will unfold in the Middle East before the Tribulation. The four signposts will all be within the Islamic realm. “This interpretation involves the four beasts of Daniel 7, the ram and goat of Daniel 8, and the four horsemen of Revelation 6,” Davidson told God Reports. “They’re all talking about the same four events, just from different aspects.” He says the first signpost was fulfilled when Iraq’s government changed between 2003 and 2005, and he now sees the Iran conflict and disruption involving the Strait of Hormuz as potential indications that the second is beginning to unfold. The second signpost involves Iran (Shia) attacking its Sunni neighbors. “At some point, Iran will destroy the rest of the Arab oil infrastructure of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE, Qatar, and Iraq,” Davidson predicts, based on his interpretation. “They’ve told the U.S. and Israel, if you attack and destroy our energy infrastructure, we’re going to do the same to all the other neighboring countries.” The attacks could be imminent, based on statements by leaders on both sides. “Iran’s threatening to do this prior to November 3 rd as an October surprise, and Trump is threatening to attack after the midterm elections. “So it could actually be quite soon where it blows up. But that’s what I see happening: the U.S. and Israel would attack Iran. Iran would fend it off like they’ve done before, destroy the rest of the Arab infrastructure, taking oil to astronomical prices.” The economic chaos and disruption could potentially threaten the US’s status as the reserve currency for the world. “Iran is going to take away the peace of mind of the entire earth,” Davidson maintains. “People will wonder how they can put food on the table.” Davidson wrote his book to warn the church because he contends the second signpost is going to be terrible. “It’s going to be awful. It’s going to change all our lives and change how we live, both in the United States as well as in much of the world. Mark Davidson “The second signpost is going to hit us in the face. I was completely aghast and flabbergasted that a U.S. president would trigger the second signpost. I was very, very surprised. “This is a whole Pandora’s box, and once the second signpost happens, that leads to the third, which leads to the fourth, which leads to the Tribulation. So, what God has done is He’s used President Trump to trigger the signpost, to trigger the coming of the Antichrist, to trigger the end of the world, and trigger Christ’s return.” If Davidson was advising President Trump, he would tell him to withdraw US forces as soon as possible. Davidson believes the rebuilding of the Jewish Temple will occur during the third signpost. He diverges from traditional teaching with his view that the coming Antichrist will be a Syrian Arab Muslim. “The ten kingdoms are not Roman kingdoms; they are Muslim kingdoms, stretching from Morocco to Pakistan,” he maintains. content:
성락교회 교회개혁협의회(대표 하재구 안수집사, 이하 교개협)가 ‘회복·감사·변화’를 주제로 ‘2026 임마누엘 성회Ⅱ’를 개최했다.

지난 11월 11일부터 13일까지 사흘간 매일 오후 8시 신길본당과 지예배당에서 참석한 성도들은 말씀과 기도를 통해 하나님과의 관계를 돌아보고 영적 재충전을 경험하며 새로운 신앙의 결단을 다졌다.

이번 성회는 로마서 12장 2절 ‘이 세대를 본받지 말고 마음을 새롭게 함으로 변화를 받아 하나님의 뜻을 분별하라’는 말씀을 중심으로, 참석이 어려운 성도들을 위해 유튜브 생중계도 병행됐다.

교개협은 ‘회복(Restoration), 감사(Gratitude), 변화(Transformation)’ 등 세 가지 핵심 주제를 통해 성도들이 영적 회복을 경험하고 감사의 신앙을 되새기며 일상의 변화를 실천하도록 하는 데 초점을 맞췄다.

임마누엘 성회 첫째 날에는 윤형식 목사가 로마서 12장 1-2절을 본문으로 말씀을 전했다. 그는 성도들이 하나님께 드리는 삶의 의미를 되새기고 마음을 새롭게 해 하나님의 뜻을 따라 살아갈 것을 권면했다.

둘째 날은 장종택 목사(코스타 강사)가 인도하는 간증찬양집회로 진행됐다. 그는 잠언 16장 2절을 본문으로 말씀을 전하면서, 세 곡의 찬양을 통해 하나님 앞에서 삶을 돌아보며 참된 믿음과 헌신의 의미를 되새기도록 했다. 간증과 찬양이 어우러진 집회는 깊은 감동을 전했다.

마지막 셋째 날에는 피영민 목사(침례신학대학교 신학대학원장)가 베드로후서 1장 1-7절을 본문으로 말씀을 선포했다. 피 목사는 성도들이 하나님을 더욱 신뢰하고 믿음 안에서 성숙한 삶을 살아가도록 권면했다.

성회에 참석한 성도들은 사흘 동안 선포된 말씀을 마음에 새기며 간절히 기도했다. 특히 각기 다른 주제로 진행된 말씀과 찬양을 통해 개인의 신앙을 돌아보고, 하나님께서 주시는 은혜를 일상에서 실천하겠다는 다짐을 나눴다.

하재구 대표는 “이번 성회는 ‘회복과 감사, 변화’라는 주제 아래 성도들이 하나님 말씀을 삶의 중심에 두고 신앙의 여정을 이어가도록 격려하는 자리로 마련했다”며 “성회가 단순한 일회성 행사를 넘어 말씀을 통해 성도들의 신앙을 새롭게 하고 삶의 변화를 이끌어가는 계기가 되기를 기대한다”고 전했다.

summary_zh: 2026年但以理祷告会第15天见证 我必施行 讲员：崔基秀牧师（江原道旌善德川教会）经文：以赛亚书46章11节“我画定了，也必成就；我计划了，也必施行。” 1. 上帝呼召我来到深山僻壤，哈利路亚！我是德川教会的崔基秀牧师，在江原道旌善深山僻壤之地牧会。第一次来我们村子的人会对三件事感到惊讶。第一，大韩民国竟然有这么偏僻的山村。要翻过好几座山才能到达村庄。村里没有公交车，快递也无法送货上门。即使只是想买一支冰淇淋，也得开车30分钟才能买到。老年人们分散居住在各个山谷中。到了主日，我会开车去接送弟兄姊妹们，每次开车都要行驶大约60公里。往返三次就是180公里。
title_zh: [2026但以理祷告会：第15天] 在山区牧会并不不幸
content:
2026 다니엘기도회 15일 간증 내가 반드시 시행하리라 강사: 최기수 목사(강원도 정선 덕천교회) 본문: 이사야 46장 11절 “내가 말하였은즉 반드시 이룰 것이요 계획하였은즉 반드시 시행하리라”.

1. 하나님께서 저를 산골 오지로 부르셨습니다

할렐루야! 저는 강원도 정선 깊은 산골 오지에서 목회하고 있는 덕천교회 최기수 목사입니다.

저희 마을에 처음 오시는 분들은 세 가지에 놀랍니다.

첫째는 대한민국에 이렇게 깊은 산골이 있다는 사실입니다. 산을 몇 개나 넘어야 마을에 도착할 수 있습니다. 마을버스도 들어오지 않고 택배도 집까지 배달되지 않습니다. 아이스크림 하나를 사려 해도 자동차로 30분을 나가야 합니다.

어르신들은 골짜기마다 흩어져 살고 계십니다. 주일이면 성도님들을 모시기 위해 차량을 운행하는데, 한 번 운행할 때 약 60km를 달립니다. 세 번을 왕복하면 180km입니다. 한두 분의 어르신을 모시기 위해 산을 넘고 또 넘습니다.

둘째는 이런 오지에 교회가 있다는 사실입니다.

셋째는 그 교회에 비교적 젊은 목사가 있다는 사실입니다.

처음 마을에 들어갔을 때 한 어르신이 저에게 말씀하셨습니다. “젊은 양반, 영업을 하려면 사람 많은 데 가서 해야지. 여기 노인네들밖에 없는데 왜 왔어?”

저는 이렇게 대답했습니다. “아버님, 아버님 때문에 제가 여기 왔습니다.”

그 어르신은 훗날 예수님을 믿고 세례를 받으셨고, 교회의 귀한 일꾼이 되셨습니다.

하나님께서는 사람이 많고 환경이 좋은 곳에만 교회를 세우시는 분이 아닙니다. 복음을 듣지 못한 한 영혼이 있는 곳에도 주님의 교회를 세우십니다.

2. 신앙의 본질을 다시 깨닫게 하셨습니다

2018년 1월, 덕천교회 전임 목사님으로부터 후임 목회자로 와 달라는 부탁을 받았습니다. 그 목사님은 일본 선교사로 부르심을 받으셨지만, 6년 동안 후임자를 찾지 못하고 계셨습니다.

저는 당시 앞으로의 사역을 위해 여러 가능성을 놓고 기도하고 있었습니다. 처음에는 선뜻 결정하지 못해 기도해 보겠다고 말씀드렸습니다.

그런데 마음에 무거운 부담이 떠나지 않았습니다. 결국 3일 동안 금식하며 기도했습니다.

금식 둘째 날, 로마서 14장 8절 말씀이 제 마음을 붙잡았습니다. “우리가 살아도 주를 위하여 살고 죽어도 주를 위하여 죽나니 그러므로 사나 죽으나 우리가 주의 것이로다”.

저는 31살에 하나님의 부르심을 받고 신학교에 들어갔습니다. 그때 저를 붙잡았던 말씀은 갈라디아서 2장 20절이었습니다. “내가 그리스도와 함께 십자가에 못 박혔나니 그런즉 이제는 내가 사는 것이 아니요 오직 내 안에 그리스도께서 사시는 것이라”.

저는 주님께서 보내시는 곳이라면 어디든 가겠다고 고백했습니다. 그러나 10년 넘는 신학 공부와 사역의 시간을 지나면서 어느새 마음이 달라져 있었습니다.

교회를 선택할 때 사례비는 얼마인지, 사택은 몇 평인지, 성도는 몇 명인지부터 생각하고 있었습니다. 어려운 시간을 견뎌 왔으니 이제는 조금 더 좋은 환경에서 사역하고 싶었던 것입니다.

그때 하나님께서 제 마음을 깨우셨습니다. 신앙의 본질은 사례비도, 사택도, 성도의 숫자도 아니었습니다. 오직 예수 그리스도였습니다. 저는 그 말씀 앞에서 회개하고 결단했습니다.

“목사님, 제가 가겠습니다.”

3. 5만 원을 통해 하나님의 살아 계심을 경험했습니다

제가 신학교에 다니던 시절에는 경제적으로 참 어려웠습니다. 학비와 기숙사비도 감당하기 어려웠고, 가족의 생계는 아내에게 맡겨야 했습니다.

어느 날 학교로 돌아가야 하는데 자동차에 넣을 기름값조차 없었습니다.

아내에게 물었습니다. “여보, 돈 좀 있어?”

그때 아내가 처음으로 어려운 형편을 이야기했습니다. “여보, 사실 아이들하고 학교에 갈 버스비가 없어서 40분씩 걸어 다니고 있어.”

그 말을 듣는 순간 마음이 무너졌습니다. 아내는 제가 더 힘들어할까봐, 그동안 아무 말도 하지 않았던 것입니다.

그날 밤 교회에서 제공한 이스타나 승합차를 몰고 학교로 향했습니다. 운전하면서 하나님께 울부짖었습니다.

“하나님, 저를 부르셨잖아요. 그런데 우리 아이들은 어떻게 합니까? 하나님, 어디 계십니까?”

그러다 자동차에 기름 경고등이 들어왔습니다. 더 이상 운전할 수 없어 여주휴게소에 차를 세웠습니다.

추운 12월 밤이었습니다. 자동차 뒷좌석에 앉아 울고 또 울었습니다. 기도조차 제대로 나오지 않았습니다. 그때 누군가 자동차 창문을 두드렸습니다. 중년의 여성 전도사님이셨습니다.

“목사님, 여기서 뭐 하세요?” 저는 기름이 떨어졌다는 말을 차마 하지 못했습니다. “조금 피곤해서 쉬고 있습니다.”

그분은 돌아가셨습니다. 저는 마음속으로 간절히 기도했습니다. “하나님, 저 좀 도와주세요. 너무 힘듭니다.”

그런데 잠시 후 그 전도사님이 다시 돌아오셨습니다. 그리고 제게 무엇인가를 건네셨습니다.

5만 원이었습니다. 저는 그 돈을 받아 들고 새벽 동이 틀 때까지 울었습니다. 그날 제게 5만 원은 500만 원, 5천만 원보다 더 귀했습니다. 단순히 기름을 넣을 돈이 생겼기 때문이 아니었습니다.

하나님께서 지금도 저를 보고 계신다는 사실을 깨달았기 때문입니다. 그릿 시냇가에서 엘리야를 먹이셨던 하나님께서 저의 작은 신음에도 응답하고 계셨습니다.

그날 저는 다시 고백했습니다. “하나님, 감사합니다. 하나님께서 저를 잊지 않으셨군요.”

4. 200년 된 집에서 새로운 목회를 시작했습니다

덕천교회에 가기로 결단한 후 아내와 함께 처음 교회를 방문했습니다.

2018년 1월, 산에는 눈이 쌓여 있었습니다. 내비게이션에도 교회가 제대로 나오지 않았습니다. 산을 넘고 또 넘어도 교회가 보이지 않았습니다.

길은 자동차 한 대가 겨우 지나갈 정도로 좁았습니다. 옆에는 절벽이 있고 고라니가 뛰어다녔습니다. 그렇게 도착한 교회는 200년 넘은 낡은 집이었습니다. 그 집에 약 6평을 덧붙여 예배당으로 사용하고 있었습니다.

처음 그 모습을 본 아내는 아무 말도 하지 못했습니다. 돌아오는 길에는 계속 울었습니다.

저는 하나님께 기도했습니다. “하나님, 저는 사명을 받았지만, 아내는 어떻게 합니까? 하나님께서 아내를 위로해 주십시오.”

아내도 3일 동안 기도했습니다. 그런데 어느 날 아내가 환한 얼굴로 나왔습니다. 하나님께서 말씀으로 위로해 주셨다는 것입니다.

요한일서 3장 18절이었습니다. “자녀들아 우리가 말과 혀로만 사랑하지 말고 행함과 진실함으로 하자”.

아내는 제게 이렇게 말했습니다. “여보, 우리가 말로만 주님을 사랑한다고 하면 안 되잖아. 이제 행함과 진실함으로 주님을 사랑하자.”

그렇게 우리는 덕천교회로 들어갔습니다. 하지만 생활은 생각보다 훨씬 어려웠습니다. 낡은 집에는 쥐가 많았고 뱀까지 나타났습니다. 천장에서는 쥐들이 뛰어다녔고, 신발 속에서도 뱀이 발견되었습니다.

예배당에는 여섯 분의 어르신이 계셨습니다. 대부분 신앙생활을 시작한 지 얼마 되지 않은 분들이었습니다. 설교 중에 서로 다투기도 하셨습니다. 그런데 1년 반이 지나자 두 분은 돌아가시고, 두 분은 요양원으로 가셨습니다.

목회가 무엇인지, 어떻게 해야 하는지 막막했습니다. 사례비도 없었습니다. 부모님과 형제들, 선배 목사님들이 보내주시는 후원금이 한 달에 약 59만 원이었는데, 겨울철 전기요금만 68만 원이 나왔습니다.

그러나 하나님께서는 그곳에서도 우리를 먹이시고 입히셨습니다.

5. 목회는 한 영혼의 삶 속으로 들어가는 것이었습니다

처음 덕천교회에 부임했을 때 가장 어려웠던 것은 지역에 깊이 자리잡은 무속신앙이었습니다. 마을에는 신성하게 여기는 나무가 있었고, 무속인들은 교회가 들어와 마을에 부정이 탄다고 이야기했습니다.

전도하러 가면 냉대받기 일쑤였습니다. 술에 취한 분이 막대기를 휘두르기도 했습니다. 저는 부임한 지 3개월 만에 지쳐 버렸습니다. 그때 하나님께 부르짖었습니다.

“하나님, 저를 이곳에 보내셨는데 어떻게 목회해야 합니까? 제 힘으로는 감당할 수 없습니다.”

기도하던 중 요한복음 21장 말씀이 마음에 다가왔습니다. 부활하신 예수님께서 베드로에게 말씀하셨습니다.

“네가 나를 사랑하느냐.”

그리고 주님은 양들을 먹이고 돌보라고 명령하셨습니다.

그때 목
